designs.isef_compliance:
CATEGORY
- ROBO, subcategory Machine Learning (fallback: SFTD Algorithms).
- Framed as an engineering project with numeric pass/fail criteria plus falsifiable hypotheses, not a demonstration or explanation model.

CONTINUATION
- Declare the June-Oct 2026 system on Form 7, with the earlier abstract and plan attached.
- The new line of investigation is counterfactual benchmarking, conformal open-set recognition and model fine-tuning, not more data with the old method.
- Board and abstract show only the new work.
- The five earlier classroom sessions and the 25-photo intent set are not presented unless the SRC agrees.

FORMS
- Research plan written by the student himself before experimentation.
- Forms 1, 1A and 1B (student and parent) signed before the first data-generating run (start date 11-07).
- Form 3 risk assessment (recommended; the work is mostly computer-based).
- Form 2A listing every AI tool, the parts it touched, and the prompt logs.
- Form 4 only for the optional classroom protocol.
- Confirm the affiliated fair's deadline content and any stricter local AI rules.

HUMAN PARTICIPANTS
- All core experiments (E1-E7) are exempt: the student researcher alone tests the app on his own apparatus photos (screened for people) and on public datasets; the user in the closed loop is simulated; no human variable is measured.
- No surveys, no teacher ratings, no classmates' data. Teacher input is limited to expert design feedback given before experimentation.
- E8 runs only if a 3-member school IRB signs Form 4 before recruitment, with minor assent, parental permission and teacher consent, adult-de-identified system-only logs, scripted non-generative outputs, and a written SRC/IRB ruling on the Companion Guide's guidance that app results are not disclosed to participants. Otherwise classroom use is ordinary teaching and nothing is collected.

GENERATIVE AI
- AI writes code only. Each module or function is marked AI-written or student-written in docs/AI_USAGE.md, with prompt logs; this ledger satisfies the rule even though the owner's commit messages must not name AI tools.
- This design document is an idea resource and is logged and cited on Form 2A.
- The student writes the plan, abstract, poster, conclusions and future work, and chooses the thresholds himself.
- The prior-art names in this design are leads, not citations. The student must read and verify every reference himself, and AI must not supply his bibliography.
- The student personally launches every data-generating run, so the AI never collects data.
- AI-made figures are labelled with the tool and date.
- Frontier APIs are used only as precomputed, logged baselines, never to generate training data.

BOOTH
- Fully offline demo with the 4B recognizer, within the no-internet rule.
- Baselines are precomputed.
- No QR codes or URLs.
- Every Commons/CC image is credited with author and licence; no images of people.
- The demo build is frozen before the Display & Safety inspection.

RESEARCH WINDOW
- January 2026 to May 2027 is respected; the new phase starts 2026-11-07.
risks: Plan or forms slip past 11-07. No experiment may run before the student-written plan and the signed forms exist. Mitigation: all code is push-button by 11-05, so the core runs fit 11-07 to 11-10; if signatures slip, drop P1/P2 items first and never drop the controls.

Few independent groups (3 source videos, a handful of photo sessions) give wide CIs and fragile in-domain conformal claims. Mitigation: group-level splits, cluster bootstrap, 1,000 random group splits checked against the theoretical Beta law, the external out-of-distribution set as an independent test, and honest reporting.

Edit-artifact shortcut: the model could learn 'smudge means change the label'. Mitigation: matched-artifact negatives in both training and test, two edit styles, a held-out LaMa edit style (P2), and natural minimal pairs (E5).

Hooke's law (and possibly average speed) has no in-domain photos, so tuning could erase the model's zero-shot ability on described-but-unseen classes. Mitigation: option dropout, monitoring on external Hooke images, early stopping on a validation group, and reporting the result either way.

The Qwen3.5 training stack on Blackwell (CUDA 12.8+, transformers >= 5.2, Gated DeltaNet kernels) may break. Mitigation: pinned ms-swift recipe, Unsloth fallback, Qwen3.5-2B fallback, or mlx-vlm LoRA of the 4B on the Mac overnight.

PEFT-to-MLX conversion, or the bf16-to-4-bit base mismatch, may degrade results. Mitigation: restrict LoRA to modules with one-to-one names, a tensor round-trip unit test, and the E7 fidelity gate (>= 95% agreement); fallback is to train directly with mlx-vlm on the 4-bit base on the Mac.

Logprobs or thinking-off may not work in the chosen local server. Mitigation: mlx_vlm.server documents top_logprobs and thinking off by default, and this is probed on 11-05; fallback is sampling-frequency scores (5 samples) for every arm.

24 GB cap: the 27B alone is an estimated 18.5-21 GB. Mitigation: one VLM at a time, an MLX memory limit, a watchdog with a fixed kill order, Bionic quit during 27B runs, and a product that uses the 4B (about 7-8 GB in total).

The server's location may block or slow Hugging Face, GitHub or Commons. Mitigation: ModelScope mirror; harvest Commons on the Mac and upload only a ~30-50 MB subset; regenerate the edits from seeded code on each side.

The student curates the external open-set test himself, so labels and selection could be biased. Mitigation: inclusion criteria and pools are fixed in the plan before any model output is seen, and every rejection reason is logged.

Human-participant violation if classmates use the app during the 11-07 practice and anything from it is reported. Mitigation: no core claim needs humans; classroom use happens only as ordinary teaching or under an IRB.

Judges may challenge the novelty, since counterfactual tuning and conformal prediction already exist. Mitigation: claim only the combination, domain and evaluation (physics-derived identifiability, matched-artifact controls, an open-set guarantee on-device), and cite CSS, CF-VLM, Stutz et al. and Silva-Rodriguez et al. after the student has read them.

AI-integrity risk: AI-drafted plan text, unverifiable citations, or AI 'collecting data'. Mitigation: the student writes all required texts, verifies every reference and launches every run; full prompt logs and the code ledger are kept.

Student time overload (writing, about 3 h of labelling, interview preparation). Mitigation: rule-pre-filled labelling UI, P1/P2 items are optional, and interview practice on conformal prediction, LoRA and McNemar continues after 11-15.
API baseline cost or provider policy changes. Mitigation: a stratified ~400-item subset, a budget cap written in the plan, and cached results.
designs.why_it_wins:
It turns the student's 'recognise any experiment' wish into a scientific claim backed by a guarantee, not a demo.

1) It is the real model-level upgrade the teacher asked for: LoRA fine-tuning of an on-device VLM driven by a physics-derived counterfactual data engine. It is tested against a data-matched control, untuned 4B/9B/27B models and two frontier APIs, all with equalised prompts and scoring, and it runs in about 8 GB on a school-laptop-class machine.

2) It shows the rigour judges score under Design (15) and Execution (20):
- pre-registered hypotheses and thresholds
- positive, negative and matched-artifact controls
- held-out source groups
- exact paired tests with Holm correction and cluster bootstrap
- a distribution-free coverage guarantee checked against its own theoretical distribution
- an honest test of where that guarantee breaks (domain shift) and how to repair it (recalibration)

3) Creativity and impact (20):
- The proven cart+track tie becomes an identifiability result: 'what you measure, not what you see, defines the experiment'.
- Digitally removing apparatus from existing photos turns the no-new-photos constraint into the method itself.
- Option dropout lets a closed-set dataset teach open-set behaviour.
- Teachers can add new experiments by description, with no retraining.
- The verified search found neither apparatus-level counterfactual evaluation of VLMs on lab setups nor conformal prediction sets for experiment recognition.

4) It is feasible and safe: every core dataset already exists; the core study is exempt from human-participant review, so it can start the day the forms are signed; it fits the 24 GB cap, the slow-upload link and the 11-14 finish.

5) It gives a strong interview and poster story with real physics thinking for a future physics/optics student. The project is an intervention experiment on a model: remove a cause, measure the effect, control for artifacts. The before/after minimal pairs with their prediction sets also make striking poster visuals.

designs.name: Lab Sleuth: Finding the Experiment You Actually Ran
designs.one_line_pitch: A 'wrong' school-lab result is an accurate measurement of a slightly different experiment. Lab Sleuth is an offline laptop app that works out which experiment the student actually ran (friction left unbalanced, a spring scale zeroed the wrong way, a pull at an angle) and names the single next measurement that will prove it. Its reasoning comes from a 9B vision-language model trained by reinforcement learning against an exact Bayesian physics verifier.
designs.research_question: Can reinforcement learning against an exact Bayesian physics verifier teach a laptop-sized vision-language model to name the systematic error behind a student's mechanics-lab data with calibrated confidence, and to choose the most informative next measurement, even for experiments it never saw in training?
hypotheses_or_criteria: H1 Calibrated diagnosis (seen experiment types). Test set: 2,000 held-out synthetic case files from the four training experiments. Claim: the verifier-trained 9B (SFT then GRPO) beats both the untuned 9B and the untuned Qwen3.8-27B, all run with the same prompt, schema and inputs, on top-1 fault accuracy (exact McNemar) and on mean log-loss (paired bootstrap, 10,000 resamples). Its 15-bin expected calibration error is <= 0.05. Every threshold in this list is a proposal; the student fixes the final values in his own dated pre-registration before any evaluation run.

H2 Experiment design. The EIG ratio is the expected information gain of the chosen candidate divided by that of the best candidate, both computed exactly by the engine. Claim: the tuned 9B's chosen next measurement reaches a median EIG ratio >= 0.8 and beats the untuned 9B, the untuned 27B and a frontier-API baseline (Wilcoxon signed-rank). In 500 closed-loop episodes it reaches an engine posterior >= 0.9 on the true fault in fewer measurements than 'repeat the same measurement' (a common student default) or random choice (log-rank test).

H3 Transfer (the core ML question). Three experiment types are never used in training: momentum conservation, mechanical-energy conservation and simple-pendulum g. Claim: on these, the tuned 9B still beats the untuned 9B on accuracy and EIG ratio (Holm-corrected). If it does not, the result is reported as 'verifier training taught experiment-specific templates, not transferable error reasoning'.

H4 Reality. (a) A deliberately misspecified higher-fidelity simulator adds effects absent from the engine: pulley inertia and friction, rolling resistance, air drag, string mass, skewed timing noise and transcription slips. On 1,000 of its cases, tuned-model accuracy drops by <= 10 points relative to H1. (b) On the student's own blinded sabotage bench (target 48 real runs, minimum 24), the system names the planted condition above uniform chance over its suspect menu (exact binomial). The follow-up measurement chosen by EIG also reduces posterior entropy more than repeating the last measurement (paired Wilcoxon).

Engineering criteria (pre-registered pass/fail): (1) runs fully offline; (2) measured peak memory of everything running together <= 24 GB, with a product target <= 12 GB; (3) p95 latency <= 15 s per diagnosis turn on the M4 Pro; (4) the tuned model's raw unfaithful-statement rate is lower than the base model's (McNemar), and the checker falls back to templates in <= 10% of cases; (5) the residual physics-error rate in a blinded 200-explanation self-audit is reported with a Wilson CI; (6) no harm to photo recognition: the tuned 9B stays within 3 points of the base 9B; (7) conformal recognition sets are not significantly below 90% coverage at alpha = 0.1 on in-distribution photos; (8) the '15% relative error = verified' rule is replaced by an uncertainty-normalised agreement test.

Secondary (engine-only, exploratory): a protocol audit. For each textbook protocol it reports which pairs of faults the protocol cannot tell apart, and how much one extra measurement chosen by EIG raises distinguishability. This is a finding about the experiments themselves, independent of any AI.
designs.product_experience:
PAIN POINTS TARGETED (school mechanics labs)
- Students take one reading and stop.
- 'Human error' is the catch-all explanation.
- They cannot tell systematic error from random error, and they do not know what to measure next.
- Setup faults are invisible to them: friction balance, zero offset, pull angle, m not << M.
- A pass/fail '15% = verified' culture encourages fudging.
- One teacher cannot check every group.
Today's app mostly accepts a single trial and prints 'verified' below 15% relative error. The UI stays in Chinese for students; an English build is used at the booth.

STUDENT (laptop, no internet, no account)
1. Two doors: 'Snap my setup' (photo) or 'Pick my experiment'. The six curriculum experiments are always one click away.
2. Snap path: YOLO boxes and the existing correction canvas come first. Then a 'Which experiment?' card shows a calibrated candidate set ('90% sure it is one of these three') instead of one forced guess. If the set has several members, as with the cart+track tie, Lab Sleuth asks the one question that splits it best, e.g. 'Is a hanging weight pulling the cart over a pulley?'. If 'something else' is in the set, it names the experiment and drafts a lab card (expected relation, variables, likely suspects) labelled as an unverified draft.
3. Data table: several trials can be entered. Instrument resolutions are prefilled and editable: ruler 1 mm, the spring scale's division, and a stopwatch with a human-reaction noise model. A single trial is still accepted, but the app explains that one point cannot separate the suspects.
4. Agreement meter: e.g. 'k = 24.1 +/- 0.6 N/m: consistent / in tension / inconsistent'. This uncertainty-normalised comparison replaces pass/fail at 15%.
5. Suspect board: 4-6 cards. Each shows a friendly name, the physics name, the data signature it predicts, and a live suspicion bar (the posterior). Examples:
   - Sticky Track = friction not balanced
   - Downhill Track = friction over-balanced
   - Heavy Hanger = m not << M
   - Missing Zero = scale zeroed vertically, then used horizontally
   - Tilted Pull = pulling at an angle
   - Nose-to-Tail = distance measured front-to-rear
   - Hidden Spin = rotational KE ignored
   - Too-Perfect Twin = speed computed from the height, so the data agree better than the instruments allow (worded without accusing anyone)
   - Top-of-Bob = pendulum length measured to the top of the bob
   - Just Noise = no systematic error
6. Ghost overlay: the student's points are plotted with each top suspect's best-fit 'ghost' curve. The ghost that runs through the points glows.
7. One-more-measurement card: it names the single most informative next measurement and shows each suspect's predicted result before the student measures, e.g. 'Sticky Track: about 0.35 m/s^2; Heavy Hanger: about 0.52 m/s^2'. The student may type a prediction first (predict-observe-explain).
8. The student measures and enters the value, and the bars move. This repeats for up to 3 rounds.
9. Verdict:
   - the culprit and its size, with an interval;
   - a short explanation in which every number has been checked against the engine;
   - a side-by-side animation of the textbook experiment and 'the experiment you actually ran', whose inferred fault parameters reproduce the student's numbers.
10. Fix and verify: a quantitative fix ('raise the far end about 1.1 cm') plus a prediction for the re-run ('the intercept should become 0 +/- 0.03 N'). The student re-runs, and Lab Sleuth either confirms the fix or reopens the case.
11. Sabotage mode (practice game): the software plants a hidden fault in a virtual run. The student hunts it with as few measurements as possible, then compares the path with Lab Sleuth's.

TEACHER
1. Before class:
   - pick the experiment(s), switch individual suspects on or off, and set the measurement budget;
   - choose scripted mode (template text only; required for any research use with students) or explain mode (local model plus checker);
   - choose whether the verdict is revealed or only the evidence board is shown (assessment mode).
2. In class: one laptop per group, or the teacher's machine. Nothing leaves the room, and nothing is logged unless an IRB-approved study is running.
3. Sabotage-card challenge: the teacher draws a card and the groups race to find the planted fault.

JUDGE (booth)
A deck of 12 physical sabotage cards. The judge secretly picks a card and a fault size. The student keys in the card code, or the judge types their own numbers, and the hi-fi simulator produces a realistic data table. Lab Sleuth must find the fault offline in <= 3 measurements; precomputed scenarios are the fallback. When two suspects really are indistinguishable, the app says so and names the measurement that would separate them.

technical_components.name: Fault-Universe Engine (exact Bayesian verifier)
technical_components.what: Each experiment gets an ideal forward model and a parametric library of 4-6 suspects, always including Just Noise. Noise models come from the literature: manual start-stop timing N(0, 0.10^2 s^2), single action N(0.11, 0.07^2), resolution d/sqrt(12), ruler +/-1 mm, the Newton-2 approximation error (m+m_e)/M, and the 5/7 translational share for a rolling sphere. The engine computes: (1) each suspect's marginal likelihood, in closed form (Bayesian linear-Gaussian) when the fault is linear in its parameters and by grid quadrature otherwise; (2) the suspect posterior; (3) a fault-size interval; (4) the exact EIG of every candidate next measurement; (5) identifiability, i.e. pairs that no single measurement can separate; (6) a quantitative fix with its verification prediction. Training engines: friction, average speed, Hooke, Newton-2. Grading-only engines: momentum, energy, pendulum.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: The methods are classic: entropy-minimising next measurement (de Kleer & Williams 1987), model-discrimination design (Box & Hill 1967), BOED, Bayesian model comparison in intro labs (Blais 2020), and uncertainty revealing a missing assumption (Kok & Priemer 2023). Not found in searches (CNKI not systematically searched): a parametric systematic-error library for school mechanics experiments that combines literature noise models, evidence ranking, EIG advice and fix-and-verify, evaluated on real data. Novelty is claimed as domain + combination + closed loop, not as a new method.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Pure numpy, < 0.3 GB, milliseconds to about 1 s per case (estimate). EIG for every candidate is precomputed when the data are generated, so RL rewards are table lookups. Written by the AI 10-31..11-02 with unit tests: planted-fault recovery, posterior normalisation, EIG >= 0, near-zero EIG for an uninformative measurement, and an Occam check.

technical_components.name: Case-file generator and misspecified hi-fi simulator
technical_components.what: Generates synthetic student case files. Each has apparatus parameters drawn from school ranges, a planted suspect and size, literature noise, 1-6 trials, and student-like formatting (rounding to the division, mixed units, occasional digit slips). It also carries a suspect menu, 3-6 candidate measurements and engine labels. Splits are by experiment type: 4 for training, 3 held out. A separate higher-fidelity simulator adds effects the engine never models (pulley inertia and friction, rolling resistance, air drag, string mass, ex-Gaussian timing noise) to measure robustness to misspecification, as a proxy for the sim-to-real gap.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Simulator-generated physics data with verifiable answers already exists (Sim2Reason 2026; Mind's Eye, SimLM, LLMPhy). New here: the task is systematic-error forensics from noisy student-style tables, with a deliberate physics gap between training and test worlds.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: numpy only. 30k cases take about 0.5-2 h on the server's CPU cores (estimate); a 200-case dev set takes seconds on the Mac. Data are generated on the server from repo code, so nothing is uploaded.

technical_components.name: Lab Sleuth model: Qwen3.5-9B + LoRA trained against the verifier (SFT then GRPO)
technical_components.what: Input is a text case file; the photo is used only in the separate recognition step. Output follows a JSON schema: for each suspect, a signature type from a closed vocabulary (y-offset, x-offset, slope scale, bend at high x, scatter too large, scatter too small, drift, none) and a probability; then the chosen next measurement and a rationale of <= 60 words. Stage 1 is SFT on engine traces. Stage 2 is GRPO with a reward that combines a proper score on the true fault, the EIG ratio of the chosen measurement, signature-type accuracy, and schema validity plus traceability of every number; the weights are pre-registered. Fallback: rejection-sampling fine-tuning that keeps the best of 8 samples as judged by the verifier.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Brier-score calibration rewards (RLCR, arXiv 2507.16806, ICLR 2026) and information-gain rewards (medical interviewing, arXiv 2601.17828; elicitation, arXiv 2604.13817) exist in other domains. Simulator rewards exist for physics QA (Sim2Reason). BoxingGym found LLMs weak at EIG-style experiment design, and a 2026-10-31 search found no RL follow-up. New here: one exact verifier supplies calibration, experiment-design and signature rewards for lab-error forensics; transfer is tested on unseen experiment types; and the model runs on a laptop.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: RTX 5090: bf16 LoRA on the 9B needs about 22 GB for SFT (Unsloth figure). GRPO memory gets a day-1 probe; it should fit with groups of 6-8, <= 320 tokens and gradient checkpointing (estimate). The r=16 adapter is about 87 MB. The Mac fallback (mlx-vlm on the 9B) stays well under 24 GB.

technical_components.name: On-device serving, parity test and memory watchdog
technical_components.what: Four parts: (1) a PEFT-to-MLX adapter converter that renames keys, transposes A/B and maps alpha/r to scale; (2) mlx_vlm.server --adapter-path with JSON-schema decoding, token logprobs, thinking off by default, and an automatic check for reasoning content; (3) a server-vs-Mac parity test on 300 cases; (4) a watchdog that sums our processes' memory and, above 24 GB, kills the simplest task first.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Engineering only; no novelty claimed.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: The product totals about 9-11 GB (estimate). The 27B is used only as a batch baseline with nothing else loaded (about 18.5-21 GB).

technical_components.name: Evidence UX and Judge Challenge
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Tracker overlays dynamic models on video, but a person must build the model and nothing is diagnosed; PhET simulates ideal worlds only. Not found: automatic inference of the fault scenario behind a student's own data, overlaid on that data, with outcome predictions before each measurement.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Streamlit and matplotlib on top of the existing app; negligible memory; built by the AI on 11-04.

technical_components.name: Faithfulness checker and scripted mode
technical_components.what: Parses every number-plus-unit and the named culprit in the model's text. Each number must trace to the engine output or the student's inputs. The culprit must equal the posterior argmax, or the text must state uncertainty when the top posterior is < 0.6. On failure the model regenerates once; after that, a template is used. Scripted mode uses templates only.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Computing first and letting the model only explain is a common grounding pattern. The contribution is a measured raw unfaithfulness rate and fallback cost for lab feedback. For comparison, more than 1 in 10 LLM lab-TA answers were reported harmful (Kregear 2025), and about 20% of LLM physics feedback contained errors (Maus 2025).
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Regex and unit parsing; trivial memory.

technical_components.name: Evaluation harness, pre-registration and AI ledger
technical_components.what: One harness runs every arm with the same prompt, schema, inputs and decoding budget. Statistics: exact McNemar, paired bootstrap, Wilcoxon, Wilson intervals, ECE with bootstrap CI, Holm-Bonferroni, Kaplan-Meier with log-rank. Frontier-API baselines are cached. The student writes a dated pre-registration. docs/AI_USAGE.md maps every file and function to its author and links the prompt logs.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Good practice (measure before building), not novelty.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Python/numpy/scipy; built by the AI on 11-03.

technical_components.name: Calibrated recognition: conformal sets, one EIG question, open-set draft lab card
technical_components.what: Scores the 6 curriculum experiments plus 'other' by combining YOLO rules with VLM token logprobs. Split-conformal sets at alpha = 0.1 are calibrated on splits grouped by source. A bank of 10-15 questions with answer likelihoods is kept; the question with the highest EIG over the current set is asked. For 'other', the VLM drafts a lab card (expected relation, variables, suspects), and the generic signature engine analyses the data against that relation.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Conformal prediction for zero-shot VLMs (CVPR 2025) and clarifying questions under ambiguity (CLAM) exist. Not found: coverage-guaranteed sets plus active questioning for experiment-type recognition from setup photos. This turns the proven cart+track tie into a measured feature.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Logprobs come from mlx_vlm.server; everything else is numpy; minutes of compute.

technical_components.name: Generic signature engine (open-set data analysis)
technical_components.what: Experiment-agnostic model comparison of the ideal relation against each signature family (offsets, scale, bend, inflated or deflated scatter, drift), with EIG computed over the signature families. Open-set experiments therefore still get evidence bars and a next-measurement suggestion, e.g. measure near x = 0 to separate an offset from a scale error.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Residual diagnostics and BIC are standard statistics. New here: one closed signature vocabulary shared by the engine, the model's output and the UI, which serves as the scaffold for transfer to unknown experiments.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: numpy; trivial.

technical_components.name: Equipment-level minimal-pair audit
technical_components.what: Starting from existing YOLO boxes, mask one decisive item (dynamometer, second cart, hanging mass or string) with OpenCV inpainting, and mask a same-size control region. Then check that the recognition set changes exactly as physics requires.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Minimal-pair evaluation exists (Winoground, MMVP, NaturalBench). Not found: equipment-level counterfactual pairs for lab setups.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: OpenCV on existing images; no new photos needed; < 1 GB.

technical_components.name: Real sabotage bench (student researcher alone)
technical_components.what: A script-randomised schedule of physical or bookkeeping faults in real apparatus (Hooke, sliding friction, average speed). Data are frozen before diagnosis. For each run, both the EIG-chosen follow-up and a plain repeat are measured. The bench also measures how much a spring scale's zero shifts between vertical and horizontal use, for which no literature value was found. Reaction-time and elastic-limit faults are simulated only.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Fault injection is a classic validation method. Not found: using it to validate an AI lab diagnoser on real school apparatus.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Basic school or home kit; about 10 min per run (estimate); 24 runs by 11-12 and 48 by December.

technical_components.name: Stretch: all-experiment deployment model, 27B QLoRA, IRB-gated classroom phase
technical_components.what: Three stretch items: (1) retrain on all 6 curriculum experiments plus the pendulum for deployment; (2) apply the same recipe as QLoRA on Qwen3.8-27B to test what model scale adds; (3) run E7 only after IRB approval.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Adds a scale comparison and field evidence; no new method.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Unsloth says 27B QLoRA fits in 24 GB of VRAM, but its Qwen3.5 guide advises against QLoRA for this family. MLX conversion is unproven, and serving the 27B takes about 18.5-21 GB. It is deployed only if it passes the parity test and the 24 GB cap.

designs.model_upgrade:
WHAT IS TRAINED
A LoRA adapter on Qwen3.5-9B: rank 16, alpha 32, all linear layers of the language model, vision tower frozen. Qwen3.5-9B is an official Apache-2.0, natively multimodal model; its MLX 4-bit build is 5.98 GB. Training data are text only, because no labelled photos of faulty setups exist and none can be taken. The photo is used only by the separate recognition step.

Model input: a case file containing the experiment, instrument resolutions, the student's data table, a suspect menu and 3-6 candidate measurements.

Model output (JSON schema):
- for each suspect, a signature type from a closed vocabulary (y-offset, x-offset, slope scale, bend at high x, scatter too large, scatter too small, drift with trial order, none) and a probability;
- the chosen next measurement;
- a rationale of <= 60 words.

Stage 1, SFT on about 12k engine traces. Targets: the exact posterior (rounded), the EIG-optimal measurement, the true signature types and a templated evidence rationale.

Stage 2, GRPO on about 4k prompts (groups of 6-8, <= 320 new tokens, thinking off). The reward has four terms; the student fixes the weights w1-w4 in the pre-registration:
- w1 x proper score of the true fault (clipped log score, or 1 - multi-class Brier/2);
- w2 x EIG(chosen) / EIG(best);
- w3 x signature-type accuracy;
- w4 x schema validity and traceability of every number.
All rewards are exact lookups into precomputed engine outputs. Because the scores are proper, the report that maximises expected reward is the Bayesian posterior. That makes calibration an explicit training target, and the RL target agrees with the SFT target in expectation.

Fallback: rejection-sampling fine-tuning (sample 8, keep the one the verifier rates best, one SFT pass).

DATA SOURCE
All data are generated by code on the server, so nothing is uploaded. No frontier-API output is used in training, which keeps the baselines independent and avoids teacher contamination. Split by experiment type:
- train: friction, average speed, Hooke, Newton-2;
- held out for H3: momentum, energy, pendulum.

COMPUTE LOCATION
A rented RTX 5090 from the day the forms are signed (target 11-06 evening) to about 11-10. Fallback: mlx-vlm SFT/RFT of the 9B on the Mac, which stays well under 24 GB but is slower.

DEPLOYMENT PATH
1. Download only the adapter (about 87 MB) to the Mac.
2. A custom PEFT-to-MLX converter renames keys, transposes A/B and maps alpha/r to scale.
3. Serve with mlx_vlm.server --adapter-path on the Qwen3.5-9B MLX 4-bit base, with JSON-schema decoding and token logprobs. Thinking is off by default, and this is checked automatically.
4. Optionally fuse the adapter into the 4-bit MLX model and import it into LM Studio.
Merged 16-bit weights are never transferred.

In the product:
- For the six curriculum experiments, the UI shows the exact engine posterior; the model supplies the wording and handles messy input.
- For any other experiment, the model's judgement is shown, labelled as a learned estimate, next to the generic signature engine's statistics.
In short: train where exact verifiers exist, and deploy the model where they do not.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
E1-E4 compare the tuned model against:
- the untuned 9B, with thinking off and with thinking on (a stronger, more compute-hungry baseline);
- the untuned Qwen3.8-27B;
- the 9B with SFT only, and GRPO without the calibration term or without the EIG term;
- the engine as an oracle upper bound;
- rule, random and 'repeat' policies;
- a precomputed frontier-API baseline.
Also measured: a Mac-vs-server parity test (300 cases; accuracy difference and Cohen's kappa) and no-harm checks on photo recognition (E5) and explanation faithfulness (E6).

STRETCH (P2)
The same recipe as QLoRA on Qwen3.8-27B. It is adopted only if it fits within 24 GB on the Mac and passes the parity test.

experiments.name: E1 Calibrated diagnosis on seen experiment types (tests H1)
experiments.data: 2,000 synthetic case files, 500 per training experiment (friction, average speed, Hooke, Newton-2), with new seeds and parameter draws. Stratified by suspect (Just Noise included) and by number of trials (1, 2, or 3-6). A separate 1,000-case validation set is used only for early stopping.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Engine oracle (upper bound). Rule baseline: the current 15% rule plus a textbook error checklist. Qwen3.5-9B base, with thinking off and with thinking on. Qwen3.8-27B base, as a 4-bit build on the server plus a 300-case MLX parity subset on the Mac. 9B-SFT. 9B-SFT+GRPO (main arm). If GPU time allows, two ablations: GRPO without the calibration term, and GRPO without the EIG term. Frontier-API baseline on a 500-case stratified subset, with the same prompt and schema, precomputed.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Metrics: top-1 fault accuracy; mean log-loss and Brier score of the true suspect; 15-bin ECE with a reliability diagram; KL divergence to the engine posterior; fault-size error. Tests: exact McNemar for paired accuracy; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples) with 95% CIs for differences in log-loss, Brier and ECE; Wilson CIs; Holm-Bonferroni across the pre-registered primary family.
experiments.sample_size: 2,000 test cases. Estimated power is about 0.85 to detect a 3-point paired accuracy difference at alpha 0.05, assuming about 20% discordant pairs. The API subset is 500 cases; it has lower power, so CIs are reported.
experiments.human_participants_status: None (synthetic data only).

experiments.name: E2 Next-measurement design, closed-loop efficiency and protocol audit (tests H2)
experiments.data: The E1 cases, each with 3-6 candidate measurements and their exact EIG. 500 closed-loop episodes of up to 3 measurements, in which the simulator returns outcomes under the planted fault. A protocol audit that simulates 1,000 classes per fault under each textbook protocol.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: EIG-optimal oracle; random choice; repeat the same measurement; fixed textbook protocol; 9B base; 27B base; 9B-SFT; 9B-GRPO; frontier API (subset).
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Metrics: EIG ratio (median and mean); agreement with the optimal choice; number of measurements until the engine posterior on the true fault reaches 0.9, computed by the engine from whatever each policy chose; each model's own final accuracy after k = 1, 2, 3. Tests: Wilcoxon signed-rank and paired bootstrap; Kaplan-Meier curves with a log-rank test. Audit: pairwise suspect confusion under each protocol, compared with the same protocol plus one EIG-chosen measurement.
experiments.sample_size: 2,000 single-step decisions and 500 episodes; the audit uses 1,000 simulated classes per fault.
experiments.human_participants_status: None (synthetic data only).

experiments.name: E3 Transfer to experiment types never seen in training (tests H3)
experiments.data: 1,500 case files, 500 per experiment. Momentum conservation: Slanted Track, rolling friction, mis-recorded cart mass. Mechanical-energy conservation: friction loss, slope length used as height, Hidden Spin for a rolling ball, Too-Perfect Twin (velocity computed from height). Simple pendulum g: Top-of-Bob length, wide swing, off-by-one oscillation count, timing noise. The engines for these experiments only grade answers and were never used in training.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Same as E1 and E2, plus the generic signature engine (experiment-agnostic statistics only). P2 sub-test: the model generates suspects without a menu; the student scores recall against his own library without knowing which arm produced each list.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Same as E1 and E2, reported per experiment and pooled; McNemar and Wilcoxon with Holm correction.
experiments.sample_size: 1,500 (500 per held-out experiment).
experiments.human_participants_status: None (synthetic data only).

experiments.name: E4 Reality checks: misspecified simulator, noise realism and the real sabotage bench (tests H4)
experiments.data: (a) 1,000 cases from the hi-fi simulator. (b) The spread of student pendulum-g values simulated under the timing model, compared with a published spread (SD 0.28 m/s^2 over 271 student values); the student must find and read that source himself. (c) The student's own real runs, each condition with 4 replicates in a script-randomised order: Hooke {control, ruler zero misaligned by a set offset, hanger mass not counted, reading from a fixed sight angle}; sliding friction {control, pull at a set angle, scale zeroed vertically then used horizontally, block mass not counted}; average speed {control, distance measured front-to-rear, initial speed from a ramp start, steep slope}. Values are typed in and frozen before diagnosis. Each run gets both the EIG-chosen follow-up and a repeat follow-up, in random order. Reaction-time faults are simulated only. The bench also measures how far the school's spring scales shift their zero between vertical and horizontal use, for which no literature value was found.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: (a) Same arms as E1. (c) Full product configuration (engine posterior plus tuned-9B narrative); tuned 9B alone; base 9B; rule baseline. Also EIG follow-up vs repeat follow-up.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: (a) Drop in accuracy and log-loss relative to E1, with bootstrap CI. (b) Ratio of simulated to published SD, with bootstrap CI. (c) Accuracy against uniform chance over the suspect menu (exact binomial); confusion matrix; Brier score; realised reduction in posterior entropy, EIG vs repeat (paired Wilcoxon); spring-scale zero shift as mean +/- SD.
experiments.sample_size: (a) 1,000 cases. (c) Target 48 runs (3 experiments x 4 conditions x 4 replicates) plus 96 follow-up measurements; minimum 24 runs by 11-12. Estimate: if true accuracy is 0.6 against chance 0.25, 24 runs give p < 0.001.
experiments.human_participants_status: None. The student researcher is the only tester, and no condition manipulates or measures a human characteristic (reaction-time faults are simulated only), so he is not a research subject. Form 3 covers masses and springs: safety glasses, and the elastic-limit fault is simulated only.

experiments.name: E5 Calibrated open-set recognition and equipment-level minimal pairs (engineering criteria)
experiments.data: The existing 809 annotated images, with experiment-type labels added or verified by the student and splits grouped by source video. The 25-photo intent set is used only if its provenance is cleared. CC-licensed Commons stills and keyframes from about 110 topic-labelled CC videos (Getaclass, Physics Wikiexperiments) supply 'other' and out-of-domain mechanics images. Minimal pairs: mask one decisive item found by YOLO (dynamometer, second cart, hanging mass or string), plus a same-size control mask.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Current rules (CONFIDENT_SCORE_GAP 0.3); 9B base; 9B tuned (no-harm check); 27B base (run in batch on the Mac with nothing else loaded). Each arm is run with and without conformal sets, and with and without YOLO boxes overlaid in the prompt. Question policy: EIG-chosen vs fixed order vs random, with answers simulated from ground truth.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Top-1 accuracy; empirical coverage at alpha = 0.1 (Wilson CI); mean set size; accuracy after one question; AUROC for 'other' (bootstrap CI); counterfactual-consistency rate, decisive mask vs control mask (McNemar).
experiments.sample_size: Calibration: about 150-250 images grouped by source. Test: about 100-200 in-domain images plus 150-300 public images. 200-400 minimal pairs. All are estimates that depend on usable boxes and licences.
experiments.human_participants_status: None, provided no identifiable person appears (check every image, then blur or exclude) and every public image is cited with its licence.

experiments.name: E6 Faithfulness, latency, memory and offline operation (engineering criteria)
experiments.data: 500 explanations per arm, drawn from E1 and E3 outputs; a blinded random sample of 200 for the student's self-audit; 50 timed end-to-end turns on the M4 Pro; one full session with the network off.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Free local explanation vs checker (regenerate once, then fall back to a template) vs scripted templates; tuned 9B vs base 9B vs 27B base.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Raw unfaithful-statement rate before the checker, counting untraceable numbers or units, a culprit that contradicts the posterior argmax, and overconfidence when the top posterior is below 0.6; Wilson CI, with McNemar between arms. Also: template-fallback rate; residual physics-error rate in the blinded self-audit; p50 and p95 latency; peak summed memory; offline pass/fail.
experiments.sample_size: 500 explanations per arm; 200 audited; 50 timed runs.
experiments.human_participants_status: None. Only the student researcher does the self-audit.

experiments.name: E7 (conditional, P2, not on the 11-14 path) Classroom sabotage-card challenge
experiments.data: Anonymous group-level records only: whether each group names a fault planted in a simulated run, and how many measurements it requested. An adult collects them. No names, faces or real student measurements.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Crossover over two rounds with different faults: scripted Lab Sleuth vs a paper textbook error checklist.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Proportion correct (McNemar on groups across rounds); measurements used (Wilcoxon).
experiments.sample_size: Depends on the class (estimate 10-16 groups); exploratory.
experiments.human_participants_status: Human-participant research. Required BEFORE any recruitment: a 3-member school IRB and a signed Form 4; minor assent plus parental permission; teacher consent; Form 3; scripted output only. A written IRB/SRC ruling on showing app output is also needed, because the Companion Guide says app results should not be disclosed to participants and advises against unscripted AI responses. If approval is not obtained, the study is not run and no classroom data appear anywhere in the project.

designs.data_plan:
1. SYNTHETIC (primary, P0)
- Generated by code from the engine and the hi-fi simulator.
- Approximate sizes: 12k SFT, 4k GRPO prompts, 1k validation, 2k test-ID, 1.5k test-OOD, 1k test-HiFi, 500 closed-loop episodes, plus the protocol-audit simulations.
- Splits are by random seed, and by experiment type for ID vs OOD.
- Everything is generated on the 5090 from the repo code; nothing is uploaded. The generator code, its config and the seeds are versioned, so any case can be regenerated exactly. The set can later be shared as a reusable benchmark ('SabotageBench').
- Noise parameters use literature values that the student checks in the original sources: manual start-stop timing N(0, 0.10^2 s^2) and single action N(0.11, 0.07^2); resolution d/sqrt(12); ruler +/-1 mm; the actual divisions on the school's spring scales.
- Where no literature value exists (parallax, the vertical-to-horizontal zero shift), a wide prior is used and the parameter is flagged as an assumption. The bench measures the zero shift directly.
- Realism check: the simulated spread of pendulum-g values is compared with a published student distribution (E4b).

2. REAL NUMBERS (P1)
- The student's own sabotage-bench tables: typed values only, no photos.
- The randomisation schedule is generated by script and committed before each session.
- Data are frozen before diagnosis.

3. EXISTING IMAGES (P1)
- 809 annotated images: 241 photos plus 568 frames from 6 videos. The server pulls data/dataset.zip from the public repo; the Mac copy is downloaded only with the user's approval.
- Before use:
  - check every image for identifiable people, and blur, crop or exclude;
  - check the licence and provenance of the six source videos before any frame goes on the poster, because the frame filenames look like downloaded web videos;
  - the student adds or verifies experiment-type labels (the AI may pre-suggest them from file names, which is disclosed).
- The 25-photo intent set is used only if the student captured it himself with no classmates' data, or if it is certified de-identified.
- The earlier five classroom sessions are never used as ISEF data.

4. PUBLIC DATA (P1)
- Wikimedia Commons stills, plus keyframes from the Getaclass (CC BY 3.0) and Physics Wikiexperiments (CC BY-SA 4.0) videos.
- Fetched as 960/1280 px thumburls through the API, with at most 200 requests per minute, at most 2 parallel media downloads, and sha1 de-duplication.
- Each item gets a manifest row: title, author, URL, licence.
- Optional distractor images on the server only: PhysiSens and the Figshare lab-equipment set, both CC BY 4.0.
- The student verifies the labels, and every item is cited.

5. WHAT LEAVES THE MACHINE
- Only synthetic case files are sent to the frontier-API baselines; no photos and no student data.
- Every model call, local or API, is logged with prompt, response, model, settings and seed, for reproducibility and Form 2A.

6. STORAGE
- Results, seeds, the pre-registration and the notebooks are kept in git with dated commits. Commit messages stay tool-neutral; the AI ledger records authorship.
- Server datasets are deleted when the rental ends; only summaries and the adapter are kept.
designs.compute_and_memory_plan:
MAC (M4 Pro, 48 GB unified memory; hard cap of 24 GB for everything running together)

Before 11-06 (AI only, light):
- Code, pure-numpy unit tests (< 1 GB, < 1 min each) and 200-case dev sets (seconds). No model is loaded.
- Only with the user's approval: download Qwen3.5-9B MLX 4-bit (5.98 GB) and dataset.zip, then run a 5-case JSON-format smoke test. Its outputs are discarded and logged as debugging, not data.
- Disk: the 9B (about 6 GB) plus Qwen3.8-27B MLX 4-bit (16.08 GB) take about 22 GB of the roughly 39 GB free. A fused copy of the 27B is never stored.

Product runtime after 11-06 (all estimates, to be measured):

| Component | Memory |
|---|---|
| Tuned 9B via mlx_vlm.server: weights | about 6 GB |
| Tuned 9B: KV cache and transients | 1-2 GB |
| YOLOv8s | 0.3-0.6 GB |
| Streamlit | about 0.5 GB |
| Engine | < 0.3 GB |
| Browser | about 1 GB |
| Total | about 9-11 GB |

- Latency (estimate, not yet measured): 9B decode about 30-45 tok/s and prefill a few hundred tok/s, so about 5-8 s per diagnosis turn.

27B baseline runs (Qwen3.8-27B):
- Runs alone with nothing else open: about 18.5-21 GB with 8k context and one image downscaled to <= 1024 px. Thinking off is verified.
- A 300-case text parity subset at about 15-20 s per case takes about 1.5-2 h. Photo recognition on about 400 images at about 10 s each takes about 1 h. Both run overnight 11-08/11-09.
- Check memory first with 'lms load --estimate-only' or the mlx equivalent.

Memory watchdog:
- Polls every 2 s and sums the RSS/phys_footprint of our processes.
- Above 24 GB it stops the simplest task first, in this order: browser preview, Streamlit, YOLO worker, and the model server last.
- MLX processes are also started with mx.set_memory_limit.

RTX 5090 (32 GB), rented from the evening the forms are signed (target 11-06, latest 11-07) until about 11-10

- Bootstrap: install PyTorch built for CUDA 12.8+ (needed for sm_120). Pull the code and dataset.zip from GitHub. From Hugging Face, or the ModelScope mirror if it is blocked, pull:
  - Qwen3.5-9B bf16 (about 18-19 GB, estimate);
  - Qwen3.5-0.8B for the dry run;
  - a 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B build for the text baselines: NVFP4 (about 22-23 GB) or GGUF Q4_K_M with llama.cpp.
- Data generation: 30k cases with exact EIG, about 0.5-2 h on all CPU cores (estimate).
- SFT: bf16 LoRA r=16, about 22 GB VRAM (Unsloth's figure for the 9B), about 1-2 h (estimate).
- GRPO: run a memory probe on day 1 (groups of 6-8, 256-320 tokens, gradient checkpointing). If vLLM lacks the hybrid architecture, use HF generate. About 2.5-6 h for about 500 steps (estimate).
- GRPO fallbacks: RFT (about 2-3 h), or Qwen3.5-4B as the backup model (about 10 GB for bf16 LoRA).
- Evaluation of all arms on all test sets: hours, not days (estimate). The 27B text baselines run on the 4-bit server build; the quantisation difference is stated and cross-checked against the Mac MLX parity subset.
- Returned to the Mac: only the adapter (about 87 MB; about 15 min even at 100 KB/s) and the result JSON files.

FRONTIER API
Run once over about 1,000 synthetic cases per model (500 ID + 500 OOD) and cached. It is never called by the product or at the booth.
