designs.isef_compliance:
CATEGORY
- ROBO, Machine Learning. Alternative: Cognitive Systems. Fallback: SFTD-Algorithms.
- Framed as hypotheses plus engineering criteria with quantitative tests and statistics, not as a demonstration or explanation model.

FORMS AND ORDER
- Before any experimentation (evaluation data, training runs, bench runs) the following must be done:
  - research plan, in the student's own words;
  - Form 1 (Adult Sponsor);
  - Form 1A;
  - Form 1B (student and parent);
  - Form 3 (risk: masses and springs; safety glasses).
- The new ISEF phase starts on that date, inside the 12-month window.
- Form 7 (continuation):
  - The June-Oct 2026 system (YOLO + rules + API explanation, entered in other competitions and a journal) is prior work.
  - The substantive new line of investigation is: verifier-trained error forensics with experiment design, calibrated recognition, and offline deployment.
  - The board and abstract show only the new work; the previous abstract and plan are attached.
- Form 2A: list of AI tools and full prompt logs.
- Form 4: only for Path A.
- Form 2C for a rented GPU: probably not needed, but the rules do not say, so ask the SRC.
- The plan must list every phase, because nothing can be added after the affiliated fair.

HUMAN PARTICIPANTS
- E1-E6 involve no human participants. They use:
  - synthetic data;
  - public data, cited;
  - existing images of apparatus only, checked for identifiable people;
  - testing by the student researcher alone, with no human variable (reaction-time faults are simulated only).
- Nobody else uses or tests the app for the study. No teacher ratings and no surveys.
- The earlier five classroom sessions, and any classroom use from 11-07 on, are not reported.
- Path A (an IRB-approved study, later) requires all of the following before recruitment:
  - a 3-member IRB: an educator who is not the sponsor, an administrator, and a medical or mental-health professional;
  - Form 4 signed;
  - assent plus parental permission, and adult consent;
  - scripted output only;
  - de-identified group-level data, collected by an adult;
  - a written ruling on whether app output may be shown to participants.
- Path B (the default for November): the teacher may use the software as ordinary teaching practice, but nothing is recorded and nothing goes into the project.

GENERATIVE AI (RULE 8)
- This design and nearly all of the code are AI-assisted. Log every prompt, including this workflow and both coding assistants, for Form 2A.
- Keep docs/AI_USAGE.md, which maps each file and function to its author (AI or student). Commit messages stay tool-neutral under the user's rule, so the ledger is where AI-written code is identified.
- The student personally writes the research plan, the pre-registration thresholds, the abstract, poster and paper, the conclusions and the future work. Do not paste this design into the plan.
- AI must not supply citations or a starting bibliography. Every source named in AI material is only a lead; the student must find it, read it and cite it himself.
- The hypotheses here are idea-development suggestions. He must restate, modify and own them, and disclose where they came from.
- Credit code-made figures (e.g. 'created by the finalist with matplotlib, 2026') and record their AI-written plotting code in the ledger.

FRONTIER API
- Used only as a baseline, with synthetic inputs only, and precomputed.
- Never used in the product or at the booth.
- Described generically in the abstract and cited in the plan.

BOOTH
- The demo runs fully offline on the laptop, and the build is frozen after the Display & Safety inspection.
- Confirm that a live offline demo is acceptable; playback of precomputed scenarios is the fallback.
- No QR codes, URLs or email addresses. The poster stands without power. The sabotage cards are paper.
- Credit every image (Commons licences, videos), blur any person, and keep consent forms out of the hall.
risks: GRPO may not fit in memory, or may be unstable, on the hybrid Qwen3.5-9B (it uses Gated DeltaNet kernels, and vLLM support is unknown). Mitigation: a day-1 memory probe; an HF-generate path; RFT as fallback; Qwen3.5-4B as backup model; Mac-native mlx-vlm SFT/RFT if the 5090 is unavailable.

Judges may object: 'you trained and tested on your own simulator'. Mitigation: held-out experiment types (H3); a deliberately misspecified hi-fi test world (H4a); a real blinded bench (H4b); noise calibrated to the literature and checked against a published distribution; the engine is reported only as an oracle upper bound, never as reality.

The tuned 9B may not beat the untuned 27B or the frontier API. Mitigation: pre-registered criteria and honest reporting. The product still works because the exact engine covers the curriculum experiments, and 'what RL adds over SFT, and what scale adds' is itself a result.

Adapter transfer and quantisation mismatch: training is bf16 but serving is MLX affine 4-bit. Mitigation: converter unit tests; a 300-case parity test; fall back to training natively on the Mac or to a fused MLX model; never move merged weights.

Disqualification through human-participant work or AI misuse. Mitigation: a core study with no participants; Path B by default; IRB approval before any recruitment; plan, abstract and poster written by the student; full prompt logs and code ledger; no AI-supplied citations.

Experiments must come after the forms, so late signatures delay every heavy run. Mitigation: collect signatures on 11-06. All tooling is ready by 11-05, so the heavy runs still fit in 11-07..11-10 even if they start a day late.

Student time and understanding: 9 days to write, get forms signed, run the bench and master AI-written code, with the interview worth 25 points. Mitigation: the AI finishes tooling by 11-05; daily walkthroughs; he codes one fault model by hand; the bench minimum is 24 runs; a mock interview on 11-13; the variant schedule if 11-15 needs only forms.

Going over the 24 GB memory cap on the Mac when the 27B runs alongside the UI. Mitigation: the product uses only the 9B; the 27B runs only in batch with nothing else loaded; the watchdog stops the simplest task first; images <= 1024 px; 8k context.
Network at the rented server: Hugging Face or GitHub may be blocked or slow. Mitigation: ModelScope mirror; only small artefacts move (the adapter of about 87 MB and JSON results).

Local serving quirks: thinking-mode text leaking into replies (an open LM Studio bug), or invalid JSON. Mitigation: mlx_vlm.server with thinking off by default; schema-constrained decoding; an automatic check that the reply contains no reasoning text; template fallback.

Some fault pairs cannot be told apart from the data, e.g. a pure scale fault versus a different true constant. Mitigation: the engine computes identifiability; the UI says so and names the measurement that would separate them; the result is reported as a protocol-audit finding.

Data provenance: the six source videos may be web downloads, and the 25-photo set may come from classroom sessions. Mitigation: check licences and provenance; exclude the material or obtain written certification that it is de-identified; never show unlicensed frames.

Bench bias: the student knows which fault was planted. Mitigation: script-randomised order; identical procedure on every run; data frozen before diagnosis; both follow-ups measured; the limitation stated.

Novelty challenge: every component has prior art (GDE, BOED, BoxingGym, Sim2Reason, RLCR, information-gain RL in dialogue, PhysicsAssistant). Mitigation: claim the domain, the combination, the transfer test and the closed loop as new; show a prior-art map that marks exactly what is new.
designs.why_it_wins:
CREATIVITY AND IMPACT (20 points)
- It changes what a lab AI is for: it designs the next experiment instead of handing out an answer. Instead of 'error 18%', it says which slightly different experiment the data came from and which one measurement will prove it.
- Suspect boards, ghost curves, the 'experiment you actually ran' animation and sabotage cards make Bayesian evidence visible and playful for 14-17-year-olds.
- The closest existing system is PhysicsAssistant (YOLOv8 + GPT for 8th-grade labs). It explains; it does not diagnose errors or design measurements. No school-lab system that combines fault libraries, evidence ranking and next-measurement design was found.
- It is offline, private and free. A 9B model fits a 16 GB school laptop, no student data leaves the room, and it extends a teacher's diagnostic expertise to every group.

A REAL MODEL-LEVEL UPGRADE, AS THE TEACHER REQUIRES
- A LoRA-trained VLM is rewarded by an exact verifier, through proper scoring rules (for calibration) and exact EIG (for experiment design), and its transfer to unseen experiments is tested.
- This targets a documented weakness, not just wrapping a model in an app: BoxingGym showed LLMs struggle at EIG-style experiment design.
- It turns the 'no new photos' constraint into a design argument. The bottleneck is verifiable reasoning data, which code can generate without limit; photos are only needed for recognition.

SCIENCE (research question 10 + design 15 + execution 20 points)
- Pre-registered hypotheses, with ground truth known by construction.
- Paired tests with multiplicity control and power estimates.
- Held-out experiment types, plus a deliberately misspecified test world.
- A real blinded bench.
- A protocol audit that is a physics-education result in its own right: which textbook protocols cannot diagnose their own errors, and the single measurement that fixes this.
- It answers the Chinese curriculum requirement to analyse experimental errors and propose ways to reduce them, and it replaces the 15% pass/fail rule with an uncertainty-based comparison. Physics-education research the student should read for himself supports this.

INTERVIEW (25 points)
The student can win the room live: 'Pick a card and sabotage my experiment' turns the 15 minutes into an experiment the judge runs. He can:
- derive every signature on a whiteboard: a = (mg - f)/(M + m), the (m + m_e)/M bend, the 5/7 rolling share, the timing bias, and EIG for a two-suspect case;
- answer the hardest question, 'why train a model if you have an exact engine?': train where verifiers exist, deploy where they do not, and H3 measures exactly that;
- explain why proper scoring rules force honest probabilities;
- show the fault model he coded by hand;
- present failure cases and identifiability limits candidly.
These cover every interview criterion: clear answers, the underlying science, limitations, independence, impact and further research.

COMPLIANCE AS A QUIET ADVANTAGE
The core study has no human participants and the AI ledger is clean. That removes the two most common ways projects like this fail to qualify.

designs.name: Lab Detective
designs.one_line_pitch: A fully offline AI lab partner that works out why a student's mechanics data disagree with theory, says plainly when the data cannot tell, and names the one extra measurement that would settle it. The physics engine behind it also trains a laptop-sized vision-language model to reason the same way on experiments it has never seen.
designs.research_question: When a student's mechanics-lab data disagree with theory, how close can a laptop-sized vision-language model, trained only on physics-engine-verified tasks and running fully offline, come to the Bayes-optimal limit set by the measurement protocol in naming the systematic cause and choosing the most informative next measurement, including on experiments held out from training?
hypotheses_or_criteria: Bracketed numbers are proposals only. The student picks the final values, writes them into his own research plan, and commits them (dated, together with the test-set hashes) before any formal run.

H1 (science, identifiability): with the single reading the current app accepts, Bayes-optimal accuracy at naming the cause is low [proposed: < 50% averaged over the 6 experiments]. Even under the standard multi-point worksheet, at least one cause pair per experiment stays confounded [pairwise Bayes accuracy < 0.6]. One EIG-chosen extra measurement raises Bayes-optimal accuracy by [>= 20] pp. Falsified if the standard worksheet already separates every cause.

H2 (engine): on simulated data the Bayesian engine lands within [3] pp of the oracle when its noise model is correct and loses <= [10] pp under noise misspecification. False alarms on clean data stay <= [10]%, and >= [70]% of unmodelled-fault controls get flagged 'cause not in my list'.

H3 (experimental design): one EIG-chosen extra measurement raises the posterior of the true cause more than repeating the same measurement or picking a random menu item (paired Wilcoxon, Holm-corrected p < 0.05). This must hold both in simulation and in the student's real runs.

H4 (model upgrade, primary): on the 4 held-out experiments, the engine-trained Qwen3.5-4B (S2) beats its own base on top-1 cause accuracy (exact McNemar, Holm-corrected p < 0.05), reaches >= [70]% of oracle accuracy, and has lower EIG-regret. GRPO (S3) transfers at least as well as engine-target SFT (S1), which is what outcome-reward RL results predict (Chu et al., ICML 2025).
H5 (laptop tier): the best 4B is non-inferior to the 27B zero-shot on in-distribution diagnosis (margin [3] pp) while using <= 1/4 of its memory.

H6 (faithfulness): verifier-flagged unsupported or wrong claims appear in <= [5]% of the trained 4B's explanations, fewer than both base models. Against the student's blinded audit, the verifier reaches precision >= [0.9] and recall >= [0.8].

H7 (data-use control): when the rows of the data table are shuffled, every arm's accuracy falls to within [5] pp of the prior rate. This shows the decisions come from the data, not from the experiment name.

H8 (recognition, P1): split-conformal candidate sets reach >= [90]% empirical coverage. Set-of-Mark plus configuration cues resolve >= [80]% of the cart+track ties the rule classifier leaves. Masking the decisive apparatus flips the label at least [40] pp more often than masking an equal-area control region.
EC1 Offline: every function works with networking disabled; no external API is called inside the product.
EC2 Memory: peak resident memory of everything we run <= 24 GB on the workstation tier (27B) and <= 8 GB on the laptop tier (4B).
EC3 Latency [proposed]: engine diagnosis < 1 s; laptop-tier diagnosis plus explanation < 15 s; workstation recognition < 30 s per photo.

EC4 >= 99% schema-valid model outputs. EC5 Manual selection of the six curriculum experiments is always available and never overridden. EC6 >= 95% identical top-1 between the server build and the Mac build of the adapter (200-case parity test).
designs.product_experience:
STUDENT. The laptop tier is the default; the workstation tier runs on the 48 GB Mac. The UI is in Chinese, with an English toggle for the booth.
1. Open Lab Detective with networking off. Choose 'Identify from photo', or pick one of the six curriculum experiments directly. The manual menu stays one click away on every screen, and whatever the student picks there is never overridden.
2. Photo path: YOLO draws numbered boxes, and the student can correct them on the existing canvas. The local VLM returns a structured guess (one of the six, or a named other experiment such as 'simple pendulum'), the configuration cues it relied on ('string over a pulley to a hanging mass', 'track tilted'), and a calibrated candidate set. With one candidate, the student confirms or changes it. With several (the cart+track three-way tie), the app asks the single yes/no question that best splits them, e.g. 'Is a hanging mass pulling the cart?'
3. Unregistered experiment: the app says it has no physics model for this one and offers a generic data table using the variables the model proposes. Every later output is labelled 'AI estimate - not physics-verified'.
4. Predict (optional, predict-observe-explain style): before seeing results, the student ticks the cause they suspect. The choice stays on the device.
5. Enter data in a multi-point table (e.g. acceleration for 4 hanging masses, extension for 5 loads, final speed for 3 heights). Instrument resolutions are pre-filled from the teacher's profile. A single reading is still accepted.
6. Result card: the familiar result and relative error, plus 'consistent within measurement uncertainty?' with a z-value. This replaces the fixed 'verified if < 15%' rule.
7. Detective card: probability bars over causes ('random error only', 'friction not balanced', 'friction over-compensated', 'hanging mass not << cart mass' ...). A 'cause not in my list' warning appears when nothing fits. A counterfactual plot overlays the student's points on the curves each top cause would produce.
8. Next measurement: e.g. 'One run with no hanging mass will best separate your top two causes (expected information gain e.g. 0.8 bit, about 3 minutes).' The student does the run and types the value, and the bars update. The loop repeats until one cause dominates or the menu runs out. If the data still cannot tell, the app says so plainly.
9. Explanation: a short paragraph from the local model, built only from the engine's fact sheet. Every number, unit, direction word and named cause is checked. If a check fails, the model gets one rewrite, then a fixed template is used. Curated 'how to reduce this error' tips follow, since the Chinese curriculum asks students to analyse errors and propose ways to reduce them.
10. Export the table, plots, diagnosis and the measurement that settled it into the student's own report.
BOOTH EXAMPLE: a steel ball rolls down the track and keeps only about 71% of mgh as translational kinetic energy. The old app says 'error 29%, not verified', and the student blames friction. Lab Detective shows that friction and rotational energy (5/7 for a solid ball rolling without slipping) both fit a single angle, so it recommends one run at a different angle. The ratio does not change, so rotation wins. Measuring the ball diameter then rules out a flag-width error.
TEACHER
T1. Sets instrument profiles once (spring-scale division and range, ruler, photogate flag width) and chooses today's experiments.
T2. Protocol view, built from the atlas: a heat map of which causes today's worksheet cannot tell apart, plus the one protocol change that fixes most of them (e.g. 'add a zero-hanging-mass run').
T3. Fault-library viewer: each modelled cause with its physics, data signature and noise source. Causes irrelevant to the school's kit can be switched off.
T4. Scripted-mode switch: template-only explanations with no free generated text. This is the default in any lesson.
T5. Lessons are ordinary teaching. No class data are collected or used for the ISEF project unless a later IRB-approved study (Phase 3) allows it.

technical_components.name: labsim: executable physics twins with curriculum fault libraries
technical_components.what: numpy forward models of each measurement protocol. They cover the 6 registered experiments, plus 4 held-out experiments used only to test transfer: simple-pendulum g, free fall with ticker tape or photogate, horizontal projectile, and inclined-plane friction. Each experiment has 5-8 parametric causes taken from curriculum error lists and teacher literature. Newton-2: friction not balanced or over-balanced; hanging mass not << cart mass, with relative error (m+m_e)/M (He 2016); string not parallel; flag-width error. Hooke: total length recorded instead of extension; hanger mass omitted; ruler zero offset; beyond the elastic limit. Friction: scale zeroed vertically then used horizontally; upward pull angle; accelerating pull; peak static reading. Energy: slant length used as height; rolling friction; wheel or ball rotational energy (Kok & Priemer 2023); flag width; height-reference offset. Momentum: track not level; friction between gates; sign error; mass mis-entry; common flag-width scale. Average speed: start/stop reaction bias; wrong distance reference; not released from rest. Noise comes from the literature where a value exists: manual interval timing N(0, 0.10^2 s^2) and single-action bias 0.11 s with sd 0.07 s (Faux & Godolphin 2019); resolution d/sqrt(12); ruler +-1 mm; a 5.7% photogate-bias case. Where no value exists (e.g. the horizontal zero offset of a spring scale), the prior range is an explicit assumption and goes into the sensitivity analysis. Each experiment also defines a menu of feasible extra measurements, with minutes of lab time each, and simulates their outcomes.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: The physics of each cause is textbook or teacher literature, so it is not new. What the searches did not find is an executable, tested library of systematic-error hypotheses with literature noise for school mechanics experiments. It is the shared ground truth for every other component.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Pure numpy, well under 0.5 GB, milliseconds per simulated dataset. The coding AI writes it before 11-06 with analytic unit tests: zero-fault data must recover the ideal law, and large faults must show the signature derived by hand.

technical_components.name: Bayesian diagnosis engine with an honest 'not in my list'
technical_components.what: Computes a posterior over {random error only, cause_1..cause_K, none of these} from marginal likelihoods. These are evaluated on a grid over fault magnitude and nuisance parameters (true mu, k, g-scale), with weakly informative priors and literature noise. A posterior-predictive misfit statistic, calibrated on simulation to a fixed false-alarm rate, triggers 'cause not in my list'. An uncertainty-normalised agreement (z) replaces 'verified if < 15%', and the classic relative error is still shown. The engine emits a fact sheet (numbers, units, signs, top causes, counterfactual curves) for the explainer and verifier. GLM API calls are removed from the system.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: The method is classical: model-based diagnosis (de Kleer & Williams 1987), model discrimination (Box & Hill 1967), Bayesian model comparison in intro labs (Blais 2020), uncertainty exposing a missing assumption (Kok & Priemer 2023). What is new is automatic real-time use over a curriculum fault library, evaluated against an oracle and on real runs.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Vectorised numpy, CPU only. Estimate: 1-10 ms per diagnosis and < 0.3 GB.

technical_components.name: Expected-information-gain next-measurement advisor (closed loop)
technical_components.what: For each menu item, a Monte-Carlo estimate of the expected reduction in posterior entropy, optionally per minute of lab time. The app recommends the best item, says which causes it separates, takes the new reading and updates the posterior. A simulated-student loop evaluates the strategies. The same EIG code also picks the clarifying question in recognition.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Choosing measurements by EIG is old (GDE 1987; BOED reviews; NIST optbayesexpt 2021), and LLMs are reported to do it poorly (BoxingGym 2025). Not found: EIG advice for school mechanics labs evaluated in a real physical closed loop.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Estimate 0.1-1 s per recommendation on CPU (about 100 simulated outcomes x 6 menu items); negligible memory.

technical_components.name: Identifiability atlas: the Bayes-optimal limit of school protocols
technical_components.what: Monte-Carlo Bayes-optimal confusion matrices for every experiment x protocol: single reading (what the current app accepts), standard multi-point, plus 1 EIG-chosen measurement, plus 2. It also gives pairwise confusability, the measurement that resolves each confused pair, and sensitivity to prior ranges and noise. It serves two purposes: it is the project's physics-education result, and it is the oracle ceiling against which every model arm is normalised. Worked example the student can derive by hand: in the energy experiment with only the height varied, four causes all predict the same constant KE/PE ratio below 1. They are slant length used as height (ratio sin(theta)), rolling friction proportional to the normal force (1 - mu cot(theta)), wheel or ball rotational energy (M/(M+I/r^2); 5/7 for a solid ball rolling without slipping), and a flag-width error (k^2). One change of angle separates the first two from the last two; changing the cart mass or measuring the flag separates the last two.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Not found in the literature searched; this is the scientific core. CNKI was not searched systematically, and the student should check it before claiming novelty.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Estimate: 500 simulations per cell, 30-60 CPU-minutes in total on the Mac with a few worker processes, < 2 GB.

technical_components.name: Engine-verified fine-tuning of a laptop-sized VLM: S1 engine-target SFT and S2 reward-filtered self-training (the model upgrade)
technical_components.what: LoRA (r=16, all language-model linear layers, vision tower frozen) on Qwen3.5-4B for open-set diagnosis. Input: an experiment card (ideal law, variables, units, instrument resolution), the candidate causes, the data table, the measurement menu, and generic data-signature features that code computes for any experiment (fit of the ideal law with a free scale, slope and intercept z-scores, curvature and runs tests, residual scatter versus instrument noise). Output JSON, in this order: short evidence, probabilities over causes, next measurement, explanation of <= 80 words. A second task (20% of examples) asks for up to 6 candidate causes for an experiment as (variable, signature type, description) tuples. S1 is SFT on targets the engine writes (posterior, argmax-EIG item, template explanation). S2 is rejection-sampling fine-tuning: draw 8 samples per prompt from the base model, keep those whose reward >= a fixed threshold, and SFT on them. Reward R = format gate x (0.5 x (1 - 0.5 x ||p - q||^2) + 0.3 x EIG(chosen)/max EIG + 0.2 x verifier pass), where q is the engine posterior. The bounded Brier form follows RLCR (Damani et al., ICLR 2026), which argues bounded proper scoring rules avoid degenerate confidence. Training uses the 6 registered experiments only.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Physics-simulator rewards already exist for forward QA (Sim2Reason 2026, 5% tolerance on simulator values), for VLM world-building (PhysEvolve 2026, GRPO on engine counterfactual branches) and for physics code (RLVP 2026, which found binary rewards insufficient). Calibration rewards exist (RLCR), and STaR/RFT are standard. New here: the inverse task (cause from noisy measurements); the exact Bayesian posterior as a bounded proper-scoring target; an engine-computed information-gain reward for experimental design; a faithfulness term; and transfer measured on held-out experiments as a fraction of the oracle. This tests BoxingGym's finding that LLMs struggle at EIG-style design, within one domain.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Runs on the RTX 5090 after 11-06. bf16 LoRA of the 4B needs about 10 GB VRAM (Unsloth table), so QLoRA is avoided, as Unsloth advises against it for Qwen3.5. Sampling uses vLLM >= 0.17 (reported Qwen3.5 support), else HF generate. Estimates: S1 1-2 h, S2 2-4 h. Deployed on the Mac it needs about 3-5 GB (estimate), which is the school-laptop tier.

technical_components.name: S3: GRPO with the engine reward, plus a 9B scale point
technical_components.what: Continue from S2 with GRPO (group of 8, same reward, KL to S2) for 300-500 steps. Optionally run the S2 recipe on Qwen3.5-9B. This compares SFT, RFT and GRPO on held-out-experiment transfer.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Same boundary as S1/S2. The added contribution is a controlled comparison of SFT, rejection-sampling and GRPO in a measurement-diagnosis domain, testing the 'RL generalises, SFT memorises' prediction (Chu et al., ICML 2025).
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Unsloth's Qwen3.5 RL runs only with fast_inference=False (its own generation, slower); TRL or ms-swift are alternatives. Estimate 4-8 h overnight for the 4B, GRPO memory estimate 16-28 GB; shrink group size or sequence length if needed. 9B bf16 LoRA needs about 22 GB VRAM, so SFT only. If the tooling fails, run a second S2 round (expert iteration) instead.

technical_components.name: Fact-sheet explainer, claim verifier and scripted mode
technical_components.what: For registered experiments, the local model writes <= 120 words from the engine fact sheet. In open-set mode it writes from its own JSON, labelled 'AI estimate'. A rule-based verifier for Chinese and English extracts every number+unit, direction word (larger/smaller, 偏大/偏小), named cause and recommended measurement, and checks each one against the fact sheet. It also requires coverage (the top cause, one piece of evidence with its number, the next measurement), so a vague text cannot pass. The model gets one rewrite, then a fixed template is used. Scripted mode (template only) is the default for any classroom use.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Motivated by measured error rates of LLM lab assistants: more than 1 in 10 answers harmful (Kregear et al. 2025), and about 20% of feedback containing errors (Maus et al. 2025). Grounded generation plus checking is common in NLP; a physics fact-sheet verifier for lab feedback was not found.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: The verifier takes milliseconds on CPU. Generation estimate: a few seconds on the 4B tier, about 11 s for 150 tokens on the 27B (about 14 tok/s decode).

technical_components.name: Evaluation harness with pre-registration and levelled baselines
technical_components.what: Seeded test sets are regenerated identically on the Mac and the server; hashes are compared and files are never uploaded. SHA-256 hashes and the student's pre-registered criteria are committed with a date before formal runs. Every arm gets the same prompt, candidates, features, schema, token budget and sampling settings, with thinking off for all local arms. Controls: positive (unmodelled faults; large obvious faults), negative (clean data), and a shuffled-rows control. Statistics library: Wilson, exact McNemar, Holm, paired bootstrap, Wilcoxon, cluster bootstrap, ECE, Brier, AUROC, conformal coverage. Every local and API prompt and response is logged.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: This is method, not novelty. It follows the measurement-first discipline of the Gewu paper the student studied (rules fixed before runs, levelled baselines, positive controls), and it is what makes every number defensible.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: CPU-light; written before 11-06.

technical_components.name: Product integration, two hardware tiers and a memory watchdog
technical_components.what: Extends the existing Streamlit app. Kept: YOLO, the correction canvas, and manual selection of the six experiments. Added: multi-point entry with teacher instrument profiles; result, detective, next-measurement and explanation cards; counterfactual plots; the teacher protocol view; the scripted-mode switch. Laptop tier: 4B + adapter. Workstation tier: the 27B for recognition and explanation, always loaded alone. A watchdog polls the resident memory of every process we start every 2 s and logs the peak. Above 23 GB it kills the simplest task first, in this order: browser preview, YOLO worker (fall back to manual apparatus entry), the running LLM request (fall back to the template), then unloads the model.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Engineering. It removes the external GLM dependency entirely and is what makes the offline booth demo possible.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Estimates: Streamlit about 0.3-0.5 GB, YOLOv8s on CPU under 1 GB. The UI is written before 11-06 and only briefly launched, with the student's OK.

technical_components.name: Laptop-tier deployment path for the trained adapter
technical_components.what: A custom PEFT-to-mlx-vlm converter (key renaming, transposes, scale = alpha/r). The adapter is served with mlx_vlm.server --adapter-path, which keeps vision, JSON schema, token logprobs and thinking off. Alternatively it is fused with mlx-vlm's dequantise-add-requantise fuse into the 4-bit model and imported into LM Studio. Never use mlx_lm.fuse, which drops the vision tower. A 200-case parity test gates deployment. Fallback: SFT on the Mac with mlx-vlm, using the accepted traces the server generated (a JSONL of tens of MB).
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Engineering. LM Studio cannot load LoRA adapters, so without this path the upgrade could not run on a school laptop.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: The 4B adapter at r=16 is about 65 MB, about 11 min at 100 KB/s. Mac fallback SFT estimate 6-10 GB, never alongside the 27B.

technical_components.name: Open-set recognition with calibrated candidate sets and one clarifying question
technical_components.what: The VLM answers a JSON schema: the registered match as single-letter codes (A-F for the six experiments, G for other) so token logprobs are clean; an open-vocabulary name; configuration cues (hanging mass over a pulley, two carts facing, track tilted, dynamometer attached and horizontal); and the apparatus. YOLO boxes are drawn as numbered marks (Set-of-Mark), and images are downscaled to <= 1024 px. Split-conformal sets target 90% coverage, calibrated on a source-grouped split. If the set holds more than one experiment, the app asks the yes/no question with the highest EIG over the set. Manual override is always available. Cue-shifted priors for the diagnosis were considered and deferred, because the existing photos contain too little labelled variation to calibrate them.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Open-set recognition, conformal prediction for zero-shot VLMs (Silva-Rodriguez et al., CVPR 2025) and clarification under ambiguity (CLAM) all exist. Set-valued recognition with a coverage guarantee plus an EIG question for lab setups was not found. It targets the proven cart+track three-way tie.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: 27B: estimate 13-15 s to first token per 1024 px image, about 20 GB loaded alone. Logprobs need mlx_vlm.server, since LM Studio's documented API lists none; otherwise use sampling frequencies (Su et al. 2024). The image set is small and clustered, so confidence intervals are wide; this is stated as a limitation.

technical_components.name: Equipment-level minimal-pair test
technical_components.what: Uses the existing ground-truth boxes. Inpaint the decisive apparatus (OpenCV Telea, objects under 15% of image area) and, as a control, an equal-area box in an irrelevant region. A model whose decision follows the configuration should flip on the first edit and not on the second.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Minimal-pair and occlusion tests exist (Winoground, MMVP, NaturalBench, Zeiler & Fergus). Equipment-level pairs for lab setups were not found.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: OpenCV on CPU, no generative model. Runs on images pulled from the public repo.

technical_components.name: Phase-2 vision-side counterfactual LoRA
technical_components.what: LoRA on the 4B's vision and language layers, trained on minimal pairs with source-grouped splits to reduce shortcut reliance. Evaluated on held-out sources and the open-set images. Written into the plan for Dec-Feb.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: Counterfactual augmentation is known; equipment-level pairs for lab setups are new.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: Data-limited: the 568 frames come from 6 videos dominated by two setups (337 friction-type frames, 231 steel-ball-on-track), and there are about 241 independent photos. That is why it is deferred to Phase 2 and will be reported with honest small-n statistics.

technical_components.name: Phase-2 generic-signature engine for unregistered experiments
technical_components.what: The model compiles an unfamiliar experiment's ideal law into a typed sympy expression (variables, units), and a dimensional-analysis check gates it. The engine then applies generic error signatures (offset, scale, nonlinearity, dissipation, timing bias, outlier), turning open-set 'AI estimates' into physics-checked diagnoses. Evaluated on the 4 held-out experiments.
technical_components.novelty_vs_prior_art: LLM-written physical or statistical models checked by an engine exist (LLMPhy, Mind's Eye, automated statistical model discovery by Li et al. 2024). Generic error signatures for open-set lab diagnosis were not found.
technical_components.feasibility_and_memory: sympy plus short model calls, CPU-light. Deferred because the 11-15 window is spent on P0.

designs.model_upgrade:
WHAT CHANGES: the weights of Qwen3.5-4B (official, Apache-2.0, natively image+video; the MLX 4-bit file is 3.06 GB, so it fits 8 GB school laptops). Training adds LoRA adapters (r=16) on all language-model linear layers; the vision tower stays frozen in Phase 1. Optionally the same recipe runs on Qwen3.5-9B as a scale point. The 27B is not fine-tuned: bf16 LoRA needs about 56 GB, more than the 5090's 32 GB, and Unsloth advises against QLoRA for this family. The 27B therefore stays the zero-shot reference and the workstation recognizer.

TASK IT LEARNS: open-set diagnosis. It reads an experiment card, the candidate causes, a data table, generic data-signature features computed by code, and the measurement menu. It returns calibrated probabilities over causes, the most informative next measurement, and a short faithful explanation. A second task asks it to propose candidate causes, as (variable, signature type) tuples, for an unfamiliar experiment.

WHY TRAIN A MODEL WHEN THE ENGINE IS EXACT: the engine exists only for experiments someone has modelled. For every other experiment the product needs a model that reasons like the engine, and the school-laptop tier cannot hold the 27B. So training uses only the 6 modelled experiments, and transfer is measured on 4 held-out experiments (pendulum, free fall, horizontal projectile, inclined-plane friction). Their engines never touch training and serve only as graders. The Gewu paper's finding that SFT added little physics to Qwen3.5-9B is why the reward targets behaviours rather than knowledge: calibration, measurement choice, and faithfulness.

DATA SOURCE: unlimited tasks generated on the server by labsim plus the engine, from seeded code. No data is uploaded. Targets are exact: the engine posterior, the EIG of every menu item, and the fact sheet for the verifier. No frontier-API output is ever used for training.

RECIPE:
- S1, engine-target SFT.
- S2, reward-filtered self-training (RFT/expert iteration): 8 samples per prompt from the base model; keep samples with R >= threshold. R = format gate x (0.5 x bounded Brier match to the engine posterior + 0.3 x EIG(chosen)/max EIG + 0.2 x verifier pass with coverage).
- S3 (P1), GRPO on the same reward, with KL to S2.
Weights, thresholds, step counts and the decision rule for which variant ships are fixed and committed before training. Thinking is off; the JSON 'evidence' field is the only scratchpad, which keeps laptop latency low.

COMPUTE: RTX 5090 rented after 11-06, with transformers v5 and vLLM >= 0.17 for sampling (Qwen3.5 support reported from 0.17). Training runs on Unsloth (its Qwen3.5 GRPO needs fast_inference=False) or TRL/ms-swift, as bf16 LoRA (about 10 GB VRAM for the 4B). Estimates: S1 1-2 h, S2 2-4 h, S3 4-8 h overnight.

DEPLOYMENT: download the adapter (about 65 MB), convert it from PEFT to mlx-vlm, and serve it with mlx_vlm.server --adapter-path; or fuse it with mlx-vlm into the 4-bit model and import into LM Studio. A 200-case parity gate (>= 95% identical top-1) must pass. Fallback: SFT on the Mac with mlx-vlm from the server's accepted traces.

HOW IT IS MEASURED (E4, plus E5 and E7):
- Primary: top-1 cause accuracy on held-out experiments, S2 vs base (exact McNemar).
- Pre-specified secondary comparisons: S3 vs S2, S3 vs S1, best 4B vs 27B as non-inferiority; Holm-corrected throughout.
- Other metrics: Brier and log score vs truth, Brier distance to the engine posterior, ECE, EIG-regret, recall@6 for proposed causes, verifier-flagged claims, JSON validity, latency and peak memory on the Mac. Every accuracy is also reported as a fraction of the Bayes-optimal oracle on the same cases.
- Comparisons: 4B base, S1, S2, S3, 27B zero-shot, 27B given the engine fact sheet (explain-only reference), two frontier API models under identical prompts and schema, engine, oracle.
- Stated in advance as 'no upgrade': S2 is not better than base on held-out experiments, or better only in-distribution. That outcome would be reported as such.

experiments.name: E1 Identifiability atlas (Bayes-optimal limits of school protocols)
experiments.data: labsim synthetic data with literature-calibrated noise, for the 6 registered and 4 held-out experiments.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Protocols: P0 single reading (current app); P1 standard multi-point worksheet; P1 + 1 EIG-chosen measurement; P1 + 2. Controls: P1 + 1 repeated reading; P1 + 1 random menu item. Sensitivity: fault-magnitude prior ranges x0.5 and x2; noise x0.5 and x2.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Bayes-optimal top-1 accuracy (MAP under the true generative model) with Wilson 95% CIs; full confusion matrices; pairwise Bayes accuracy; number of confounded pairs (pairwise accuracy < 0.6, proposed cut-off); for each confounded pair, the menu item with the highest pairwise EIG; protocol differences by paired bootstrap on the same simulated cases.
experiments.sample_size: 500 simulated datasets per experiment x protocol cell and 300 per cause pair. CI half-width about +-4 pp per cell. Estimate: 30-60 CPU-minutes in total on the Mac.
experiments.human_participants_status: None; purely computational.

experiments.name: E2 Engine diagnosis accuracy, calibration and honesty
experiments.data: Frozen synthetic splits: in-distribution 600; held-out magnitudes 300; misspecified noise 300 (sigma x1.5, heavy-tailed errors, larger timing bias); clean 150; unmodelled positive controls 150 (two simultaneous causes, or a withheld cause type such as a x10 transcription slip); shuffled rows 150. Plus the 4 held-out engines.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Current app (relative error < 15% means verified; it cannot name causes); a rule checklist (intercept sign, curvature, ratio < 1) written before seeing test data; the engine with literature noise; the oracle with the true generating parameters.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Top-1 and top-3 accuracy, macro-F1, false-alarm rate on clean data, 'not in my list' rate and AUROC on unmodelled controls, Brier and log score, ECE with reliability diagrams. Exact McNemar for engine vs checklist; degradation under misspecification with paired bootstrap CIs. External realism check: the simulated spread of pendulum-g estimates against the published SD of 0.28 m/s^2 over 271 student values (Straulino 2019).
experiments.sample_size: 1,650 cases; seconds to minutes of CPU.
experiments.human_participants_status: None.

experiments.name: E3 Next-measurement advisor in a simulated closed loop
experiments.data: 600 in-distribution cases and 240 held-out-experiment cases. Each is continued with simulated extra measurements drawn from the true generating model.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: EIG; EIG per minute of lab time; repeat the same measurement (what students usually do); random menu item; fixed textbook protocol extension.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Posterior of the true cause after 1 and 2 extra measurements; top-1 after 1 and 2; number of measurements needed to reach posterior 0.9. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank and exact McNemar against EIG, Holm-corrected.
experiments.sample_size: 840 cases x 5 strategies, paired.
experiments.human_participants_status: None.

experiments.name: E4 Model upgrade: engine-verified fine-tuning and transfer (primary ML experiment)
experiments.data: The E2 splits; 480 held-out-experiment cases (4 x 120); 120 cause-proposal cases on held-out experiments; the real runs from E5.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Qwen3.5-4B base; S1; S2; S3 (P1); optional 9B-S2. Qwen3.8-27B zero-shot on the deployed MLX build on the Mac, with an optional NVFP4 build on the 5090 for the full set plus a Mac parity subset. The 27B given the engine fact sheet (explain-only reference). Two frontier API models with identical prompt, candidates, features, schema and token budget; precomputed, version strings logged. The engine and the oracle as references. Inference ablations on the base models: with vs without data-signature features. Optional: 27B with thinking on, on a 100-case subset.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Primary: top-1 on held-out experiments, S2 vs base, exact McNemar. Pre-specified secondary comparisons: S3 vs S2; S3 vs S1; best 4B vs 27B (non-inferiority, proposed margin 3 pp); all Holm-corrected. Also: Brier and log score, Brier distance to the engine posterior, ECE, EIG-regret (paired bootstrap 95% CIs), recall@6 for proposed causes, verifier-flagged claims, JSON validity, latency, peak memory, and fraction of oracle accuracy.
experiments.sample_size: About 2,250 test cases for the server-side 4B arms. 27B and API arms run on a stratified 200 per split, about 1,200 cases; at an estimated 30 s per case on the Mac, one 27B night covers about 1,000-1,200. Power estimate: with 300 paired cases and about 24% discordant pairs, an 8-pp difference gives McNemar z of about 2.8.
experiments.human_participants_status: None.

experiments.name: E5 Real closed-loop validation: the student's own blinded fault-injection runs
experiments.data: The student's own measurements on school apparatus; no photos needed. 3 experiments, chosen by kit availability among Hooke's law, friction and Newton's 2nd law (stopwatch-only setups are avoided so that no human reaction-time variable is measured), x 4 conditions (clean + 3 causes injected physically or by a sealed procedural card, including at least one pair the atlas predicts is confounded under the standard worksheet) x 2 repeats. Every run is continued with the EIG-recommended extra measurement. Condition order comes from a seeded random schedule committed in advance, and the software sees only the typed data.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Engine; 4B-S2 (and S3 if available); 4B base; 27B zero-shot; current app; rule checklist.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Top-1 against the sealed condition, before vs after the extra measurement (exact McNemar). Posterior of the true cause before vs after (Wilcoxon). Wilson CIs per arm. Simulator realism: residual scatter vs literature noise (chi-square per degree of freedom) and the false-alarm rate on clean runs.
experiments.sample_size: About 24 runs + 24 follow-up measurements over two lab sessions (estimate); Phase 2 extends toward about 60 runs with the same method. This is reported as validation with wide CIs (e.g. 18/24 gives 55-88%).
experiments.human_participants_status: Exempt as long as the student is the only person who measures and uses the software, no information about anyone else is recorded, and no human variable is studied. An adult may set apparatus conditions only as an adult procedure listed in the plan. Get the SRC's ruling in writing. If the SRC objects to the adult role, the student self-randomises with sealed cards and no other person is involved.

experiments.name: E6 Open-set recognition and equipment-level minimal pairs (P1)
experiments.data: 809 annotated images (241 photos, 568 frames from 6 videos; frames dominated by 337 friction-type and 231 steel-ball-on-track) plus the 25-photo intent set. The student labels each source by experiment and screens for identifiable people; calibration and test splits are grouped by source. Open set: 150-300 public images (Wikimedia Commons stills; keyframes from topic-labelled CC BY / CC BY-SA video lessons) with a licence manifest, labels verified by the student. Minimal pairs are built from the ground-truth boxes.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Current rule classifier; 27B plain prompt; 27B + Set-of-Mark + cue schema; the same + conformal set + one EIG question (answers simulated from the ground-truth cue table); 4B base; 4B-S2 (checks that text-only LoRA did not harm vision); two frontier VLM APIs. Ablations: ground-truth vs YOLO boxes; 1024 vs 768 px.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Top-1 on registered experiments; cart+track tie-resolution rate; unknown-experiment AUROC; conformal empirical coverage (Wilson CI) and mean set size; flip rate for decisive vs control masks (exact McNemar over image pairs); latency. Cluster bootstrap by source video or session; Holm across arms.
experiments.sample_size: About 250 independent photos plus 6 video clusters (10 frames sampled from each); 150-300 open-set images; 150-250 minimal pairs. All estimates; they depend on the labelling and the people screen.
experiments.human_participants_status: None, provided the images show apparatus only. Public images are cited with licences. Earlier classroom photos are used only as apparatus images, never as classroom-study results, and only if the SRC agrees. Anything showing people is cropped, blurred or excluded.

experiments.name: E7 Explanation faithfulness and verifier validity
experiments.data: Explanations produced by every arm in E4 and E5.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: 4B base; 4B-S2/S3; 27B zero-shot; 27B + fact sheet; frontier APIs; template.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Verifier-flagged unsupported or wrong claims per explanation; rewrite and template-fallback rates; coverage. Verifier precision and recall against the student's own blinded audit of a stratified sample (arm labels hidden), with Wilson CIs. Arm comparisons by exact McNemar with Holm.
experiments.sample_size: The verifier runs on all explanations (several thousand); the audit covers 150 (about 2 h).
experiments.human_participants_status: None. The student researcher is the only rater; teacher or classmate ratings would need IRB approval and consent, so they are excluded from Phase 1.

experiments.name: E8 Engineering criteria: offline, memory, latency
experiments.data: Scripted sessions of 30 photos + 30 diagnoses per tier, with networking disabled.
experiments.arms_and_baselines: Laptop tier (4B + adapter) vs workstation tier (27B); 1024 vs 768 px.
experiments.metrics_and_stats: Peak resident memory of all our processes from the watchdog log, against 24 GB and 8 GB; latency median and 90th percentile per stage; schema-valid rate; 100% function offline; manual-selection checklist; adapter parity.
experiments.sample_size: 60 interactions per tier (estimate 1-2 h).
experiments.human_participants_status: None.

designs.data_plan:
D1 Synthetic (labsim). Every task is regenerated from seeded code on both the Mac and the server; only code travels, and test-set hashes are compared across the two machines.
- Training pool (server only): about 20,000 prompts from the 6 registered experiments, with fault magnitudes inside the training range. Protocols are mixed: single reading, standard multi-point, and after one extra measurement. 20% are cause-proposal tasks. Labels are the engine posterior, the EIG per menu item and the fact sheet (estimate: 10-20 CPU-minutes on the server).
- Frozen test sets: in-distribution 600; held-out magnitudes 300; held-out experiments 480 (+120 cause-proposal); misspecified noise 300; clean 150; unmodelled 150; shuffled 150; closed-loop 840. Hashes and the generator version are committed, dated, before any formal run.

D2 Real runs (E5). The student's own readings, one CSV per run: run id, experiment, condition code, readings, instrument profile, timestamps. The condition schedule is sealed. No names, faces or data about anyone else. No photos are needed, which respects the 'no new photos' constraint.

D3 Existing images. 809 annotated images (241 photos; 568 frames from 6 videos, dominated by 337 friction-type and 231 steel-ball-on-track frames) plus the 25-photo intent set.
- The server pulls data/dataset.zip from the public GitHub repo. The Mac downloads it after 11-06; only about 65 images are local now.
- The student assigns experiment labels per source and screens for people.
- Splits are grouped by source. In Phase 1 the images are used for evaluation only, with no vision training.

D4 Open-set public images. Wikimedia Commons stills, plus keyframes from about 110 topic-labelled CC video lessons (Getaclass CC BY 3.0; Macedonian Wikiexperiments CC BY-SA 4.0).
- Harvested with title, author, URL and licence, within the API limits (compliant User-Agent, <= 2 parallel media downloads, <= 25 Mbps) and deduplicated by sha1.
- NC/ND items are excluded.
- Target: 150-300 student-verified images (estimate; modern school setups are a minority on Commons). Video titles count only as candidate labels.

D5 Minimal pairs, generated by code from the D3 ground-truth boxes.

D6 Literature parameter table: value, unit, source, page, and a 'read and verified by the student' tick. Values with no source are marked as assumptions and varied in the sensitivity analyses.

D7 Logs. Every local-model and API prompt and response as JSONL, with model id, build, settings and timestamp, for reproducibility and the Form 2A attachment.

NOT USED: data from earlier classroom sessions or from 11-07 lessons; any image showing identifiable people; frontier-API outputs as training data.
designs.compute_and_memory_plan:
MAC (M4 Pro, 48 GB). Hard cap: 24 GB for everything we run together. If exceeded, kill the simplest task first.
- Workstation tier: Qwen3.8-27B MLX 4-bit at 8k context plus one <= 1024 px image is estimated at 18.5-21 GB. Adding Streamlit (about 0.3-0.5 GB), YOLOv8s on CPU (< 1 GB) and one browser tab (about 0.5-1 GB) gives an estimated 20-23.5 GB, so nothing else runs alongside it. If the watchdog sees > 22 GB, drop to 6k context and 768 px.
- 27B setup: run `lms load --estimate-only` first, then `lms load qwen/qwen3.8-27b -c 8192 --parallel 1 --gpu max --ttl 900`. Turn thinking off through the native /api/v1/chat with reasoning:'off', and check automatically that no reasoning content comes back. Alternatively serve the same weights with mlx_vlm.server, which is needed for logprobs.
- Laptop tier: Qwen3.5-4B 4-bit (3.06 GB file) plus the adapter, estimated 3-5 GB with context; about 5-7 GB together with the app.
- Overnight 27B evaluations: the 27B alone plus an eval script under 0.5 GB, no browser. Estimates: about 30 s per text diagnosis and about 20 s per image, so one night covers about 1,000-1,200 cases.
- CPU jobs (atlas, engine benchmarks, closed-loop simulation): < 2 GB with a few workers, run while no model is loaded.
- Fallback training on the Mac: mlx-vlm LoRA SFT of the 4B (batch 1-2, sequence <= 1,536, gradient checkpointing), estimate 6-10 GB, never alongside the 27B.
- Watchdog (psutil, every 2 s): logs the peak. Above 23 GB it kills, in order: browser preview, YOLO worker, the running LLM request (template fallback), then unloads the model.
- Disk (about 39 GB free): the 27B (16.08 GB) and the 4B (3.06 GB), plus an optional fused 4B (about 3 GB), leave about 17 GB. Skip the 9B on the Mac unless needed, and keep >= 8 GB free.
- Light housekeeping before 11-06, with the student's OK: select the installed MLX runtime 1.13.1 or update Bionic / install LM Studio >= 0.4.26 for the developer server; `pip install mlx-vlm`. Model downloads are scheduled for 11-06, because a 16 GB download is a long continuous job.

RTX 5090 (32 GB), rented 11-06/07 to about 11-10 (3-4 days, estimate).
- Bootstrap: code via git; data/dataset.zip from the public GitHub repo (needed only for P1); weights from Hugging Face or a ModelScope mirror. Qwen3.5-4B bf16 (estimate about 9 GB); optional Qwen3.5-9B bf16 (estimate about 19 GB); optional Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 (21.95 GB) if vLLM runs NVFP4 on this card, which is unknown.
- Stack: PyTorch built for CUDA >= 12.8 (Blackwell), transformers v5, vLLM >= 0.17, Unsloth or TRL/ms-swift.
- Jobs and estimates: task and label generation (CPU) 10-20 min; S1 SFT 1-2 h; S2 sampling (8 per prompt) 1-2 h plus SFT 1-2 h; S3 GRPO 4-8 h overnight (Unsloth Qwen3.5 RL needs fast_inference=False); evaluation of all 4B arms on about 2,250 cases < 1 h; optional 9B S2 3-5 h; optional 27B NVFP4 evaluation 1-2 h.
- VRAM: 4B bf16 LoRA about 10 GB (Unsloth); vLLM sampling estimate 12-20 GB; GRPO estimate 16-28 GB (shrink group size or sequence length if needed); 9B bf16 LoRA about 22 GB. No QLoRA.
- Transfers: up is code only, since data are regenerated by the same seeded code and verified by hash. Down is the adapters (4B r=16 about 65 MB, about 11 min at 100 KB/s) and JSONL logs (tens of MB).

FRONTIER API BASELINES: small precomputed batches, about 1,200 diagnosis cases and 500-800 images per model (cost estimate: tens of US dollars). The student launches them with his own keys held in environment variables, and every call is logged. No live API calls at the booth.

designs.isef_compliance:
CATEGORY: ROBO, subcategory Machine Learning (Cognitive Systems as the alternative). The project is framed as engineering criteria plus testable hypotheses with quantitative tests and statistics, never as a demonstration or explanation model.

FORMS AND TIMING
- Before any formal run, the student writes the research plan himself. It covers rationale, question, hypotheses and criteria, materials, procedures (separating his steps from any adult step), risk, data analysis, a bibliography of sources he found and read, and acknowledgements that include AI use.
- Also before any formal run: Forms 1A and 1B signed (1B with a parent), Form 1 from the Adult Sponsor, and Form 3.
- The engineering plan may start less detailed; changes go into a dated Project Addendum.
- Form 2A: tool list plus prompt logs.
- Form 7 declares the June-Oct 2026 version (course, other competitions, journal) as prior research. The new line of investigation (error-cause diagnosis, experimental design, engine-verified model training) is the substantive expansion. The board and abstract show only the new work, and the earlier five classroom sessions are not presented as results.
- The plan lists every phase through spring 2027, since nothing can be added after the affiliated fair.
- The 11-15 requirement and the SRC rulings (continuation scope, the adult's role in E5, the intent photos) are obtained in writing.

HUMAN PARTICIPANTS
- The whole Phase-1 evaluation is participant-free: synthetic data, public licensed images, the student's own measurements and his own blinded audit. No human variable is studied; reaction-time faults appear only in simulation.
- Lessons from 11-07 are ordinary teaching run by the teacher in scripted mode. No data are collected and nothing from them is presented.
- Any study involving classmates or teacher ratings belongs to Phase 3 and happens only after a 3-member school IRB (an educator who is not the sponsor, an administrator, a medical or mental-health professional) signs Form 4 before recruitment. It needs written assent, parental permission, adult consent, scripted outputs, and no disclosure of results to participants, per the Companion Guide.

GENERATIVE AI (RULE 8)
- This design and all coding-assistant sessions (Claude Code, GPT) are logged for Form 2A.
- AI-written code is identified module by module in docs/AI_USAGE.md. Commit messages stay tool-free per the student's own convention, and the ledger carries the disclosure.
- AI must not draft the plan, abstract, poster or paper, write conclusions or future work, or supply citations. Every reference named in this design is a pointer that the student must locate, read and verify himself before citing.
- AI does not collect data. The student launches every formal run, records it in his dated notebook and interprets the results; AI debug runs from before the forms are signed are not results.
- AI may polish the grammar of finished student drafts (logged) and quiz him for the interview. Frontier-API outputs are never used as training data.

PRODUCT AND BOOTH
- No external API inside the product. Frontier APIs appear only as precomputed, logged baselines.
- The booth demo runs offline and is frozen before Display & Safety inspection. The poster stands alone without power.
- No QR codes or URLs on the display.
- Every figure is credited ('made by the finalist with matplotlib, 2026', with AI-assisted plotting code noted).
- Models are described generically in the abstract.
- Licences are recorded: models Apache-2.0, YOLOv8 AGPL-3.0, images CC BY / CC BY-SA with attribution.
- No photos of people.
risks: The trained 4B may not beat its base on held-out experiments (H4 fails). Mitigation: the primary claim is pre-registered. S1, S2, S3 and the 9B give several chances. A null transfer result, normalised by the oracle, is still reportable, and the atlas, engine and closed loop stand on their own.

GRPO tooling: Unsloth's Qwen3.5 RL runs without vLLM (slower), and vLLM support for Qwen3.5 is reported only from 0.17. Mitigation: S2 (reward-filtered self-training) is the P0 path and GRPO is P1; a second S2 round is the fallback; GPU jobs are time-boxed and checkpointed.

Adapter deployment: bugs in the PEFT-to-MLX conversion, or a mismatch between bf16 training and the 4-bit MLX base. Mitigation: bf16 LoRA (no QLoRA), converter unit tests, a 200-case parity gate, and SFT on the Mac with mlx-vlm as the fallback.
The 24 GB cap leaves only about 3-5 GB beside the 27B. Mitigation: watchdog with a kill order; 6k context and 768 px images; the laptop tier as the default demo; 27B batch runs alone overnight.

Runtime quirks: thinking-off is reported ignored on LM Studio's OpenAI-compatible path, and Bionic may not expose the developer server. Mitigation: the native /api/v1/chat with reasoning:'off' plus an automatic no-reasoning check, or mlx_vlm.server.

Simulator realism: literature timing noise comes from trained timekeepers, and some faults have no published magnitude. Mitigation: a misspecification split, sensitivity analyses, the pendulum-spread realism check, real runs, and an honest limitations section.
No lab access or teacher time for E5 before 11-10. Mitigation: E5 moves to Phase 2 with the same method, and the 11-15 claims rest on synthetic and public data, clearly labelled as such.

Server location: if the rented 5090 is in mainland China, Hugging Face and GitHub may be blocked or slow. Mitigation: confirm before renting; use the ModelScope mirror for Qwen3.5 weights and a code mirror; dataset.zip is needed only for P1.

Compliance failure is grounds to fail to qualify: an AI-drafted plan or abstract, AI-supplied citations, AI-collected data, unapproved human participants, or an undeclared continuation. Mitigation: the rules in this design, the ledger, the logs, and SRC rulings in writing.
Judge challenge: 'why train an LLM if the engine is exact?' Mitigation: the held-out-experiment design and the laptop-tier constraint answer it, and the answer is rehearsed.

Novelty challenge from Sim2Reason, PhysEvolve, GDE/BOED, BoxingGym and PhysicsAssistant. Mitigation: claim only the combination, task, reward and real closed loop, and have the student re-check CNKI/CNIPA.
Reward hacking under GRPO, e.g. vague explanations written to pass the verifier. Mitigation: the coverage requirement, the blinded audit, and reporting flagged rates for every arm.

The image data are small and clustered (568 frames from 6 videos), so recognition results are noisy and prone to leakage. Mitigation: source-grouped splits, cluster bootstrap, recognition kept at P1, and vision training deferred to Phase 2.

The student's workload in 9 days (plan, forms, labelling, lab sessions, writing, interview study). Mitigation: the P0-only path, Variant A, the briefing pack, and AI handling all code under the ledger.
Rental cost or time overrun. Mitigation: estimates up front, time-boxed jobs, small adapters, and frontier-API baselines on stratified subsets only.
designs.why_it_wins:
1) It is not a demonstration. It asks three falsifiable questions, each with ground truth.
- Science: what can school protocols reveal at all? The identifiability atlas is a physics-education finding.
- Engineering: does a Bayesian engine plus EIG advice close the loop on real apparatus?
- ML: do physics-engine rewards teach a laptop-sized VLM diagnostic and experimental-design skill that transfers?
This answers ISEF's rule that demonstrations and explanation models are inappropriate.

2) The model upgrade is real and measured against a ceiling. The weights change through engine-verified training, which is what the teacher demanded. Success is judged on experiments the model never saw, as a fraction of the Bayes-optimal oracle, against its own base, the 27B and frontier APIs under identical conditions. That is the kind of evaluation ROBO judges respect, and it tests BoxingGym's finding that LLMs struggle at experiment design.

3) The novelty boundary is clear. PhysicsAssistant recognised and explained. Sim2Reason and PhysEvolve rewarded forward prediction. GDE and BOED chose measurements in other domains. This project infers the cause from noisy school data, trains on calibrated posteriors and information gain, and tests in a real closed loop. It does not claim any single method is new.

4) It is useful and honest in class. It replaces the arbitrary 15% rule with uncertainty, says 'your data cannot tell yet - measure this', says 'cause not in my list', and gives teachers an evidence-based protocol fix. That matches the curriculum requirement that students analyse errors and propose ways to reduce them.

5) It has a memorable booth moment that runs offline: the steel ball that 'lost 29% to friction' turns out to be spinning, shown with one extra run at a different angle.

6) Compliance and independence are built in: a participant-free core, an offline booth, and a transparent AI ledger. The mathematics is something a high-school student can derive on a whiteboard and defend in the interview, which is worth 25 of 100 points.

fatal_flaws: As scoped: 24 AI-written experiment families, with only the six curriculum families physics-checked before SFT. Because generator and referee share the same code, any physics bug is self-consistent and undetectable by every metric, and the student cannot own or defend 24 fault models in the 15-minute interview (25 points; independence is scored).

scores.justification:
The most ML-novel training objective of the four: four-term counterfactual evidence tuning with matched-artifact hinge negatives and option dropout. The controls are exemplary on paper: a data-matched SFT control, a box-oracle positive control, a blank-image negative control, an option-order test, group splits, a Beta-law coverage check and a recalibration curve. The identifiability idea ('what you measure, not what you see, defines the experiment') is elegant, and the design reuses existing assets best.

The data cannot carry it. I tallied the repo label files:
- 568 frames come from only 3 source videos: 253 + 84 friction frames and 231 steel-ball frames.
- 241 photos show mostly cart and track parts. Only 4 contain a dynamometer, none contain a block or ball, and none show Hooke's law.
- Friction (2 videos) and the ball (1 video) cannot appear in train, calibration and test from different sources.
- Labels for which experiment each photo was meant for would be assigned after the fact by the researcher himself.
After deduplication the independent scenes number in single digits, so held-out-group minimal-pair accuracy and an in-domain 90% guarantee would rest on a handful of scenes. Commons has an estimated fewer than 100 modern photos of the six experiments.

Impact is weak. The upgrade improves a step the student can already do in two clicks, while physics.py's single-reading, 15% core stays unchanged. Training on, and showing poster visuals from, frames of downloaded web videos is a provenance risk. The SRC may also treat the 809-image set as prior-project data, and the claim of a new line of investigation on Form 7 is weaker because the research question (recognition) is the same as before. Prior-art citations are real (CF-VLM, NeurIPS 2025, verified) and are fairly bounded.
fatal_flaws: The data cannot support the primary endpoint or H3. The 809 images are 568 near-duplicate frames from only 3 source videos (2 friction, 1 steel ball) plus 241 photos of mostly cart and track parts (4 with a dynamometer, 0 of Hooke's law). A group split with friction in every split is impossible, so held-out-group minimal-pair accuracy and the in-domain 90% coverage guarantee rest on a handful of scenes.

physics.py's single-reading, 15%-relative-error core is left unchanged, so the end-to-end product stays a PhysicsAssistant-style demonstration: perception plus explanation. The headline gain improves only a step the student can already do with two clicks of manual selection.

scores.design: wow-product: Lab Sleuth (Finding the Experiment You Actually Ran)
scores.justification:
Best story and best booth. 'A wrong result is an accurate measurement of a slightly different experiment' is memorable, and the suspect boards, ghost curves, fix-and-verify loop and a judge sabotaging the experiment with a paper card would win the room.

The science has strong ideas:
- a bounded proper-scoring reward (RLCR, arXiv 2507.16806, verified) plus an exact EIG term;
- a deliberately misspecified hi-fi world (pulley inertia, rolling resistance, drag, string mass, skewed timing) as a sim-to-real proxy;
- a real blinded sabotage bench that measures both the EIG follow-up and a plain repeat;
- a protocol audit.
Prior-art acknowledgements check out (information-gain GRPO in arXiv 2601.17828, verified).

What drags it down:
- Transfer, its own 'core ML question', rests on 4 training and 3 held-out experiment types.
- The model reads raw tables with no shared computed signature panel, so mental arithmetic and transferable reasoning are confounded.
- H4b only has to beat uniform chance.
- An ECE of at most 0.05 is optimistic.
- P0 bundles 9B GRPO, a hi-fi simulator and a one-day UI rebuild. The GRPO is tight in 32 GB, and generation may have to go through HF generate on the new hybrid architecture.
- The student starts on 11-06 and must also complete 24-48 bench runs.
- 'Too-Perfect Twin' is an implied fabrication accusation that does not belong in a classroom tool.
- Heavy runs and AI-made tables are not assigned to the student.
fatal_flaws: The headline ML claim (H3, transfer) cannot be interpreted as designed. Only 4 training and 3 held-out experiment types exist, and the model must infer residual signatures by mental arithmetic from raw tables, with no computed feature panel and no with-panel or no-panel levelling. A null result, the likely outcome, cannot separate failed arithmetic from failed transferable reasoning. It is fixable only by adding a panel and more held-out families.

scores.justification:
The sharpest research question a physics judge could ask for: how close can a laptop VLM trained only on engine-verified tasks come to the Bayes-optimal limit that the measurement protocol itself sets?

What makes it the winner:
- The identifiability atlas is a physics-education result that stands even if the ML fails. Four causes all give a constant KE/PE ratio, and one change of angle splits them; the physics checks out.
- Every model accuracy is reported as a fraction of the oracle.
- The real fault-injection runs include a cause pair the atlas says the standard worksheet cannot separate, so the simulator makes a falsifiable prediction about real data.
- Controls are thoughtful: a shuffled-rows control on data use, unmodelled-fault and clean controls, noise misspecification, a realism check against the published pendulum spread, and a precision/recall audit of the verifier.
- SFT vs RFT vs GRPO on held-out experiments is a real ML question (Chu et al., ICML 2025, verified).
- The 4B bf16 LoRA (about 10 GB) is the most feasible upgrade on one 5090.
- Compliance is the most careful: the student launches every formal run, downloads wait until 11-06, the adult's role goes to the SRC, a Phase-3 IRB study is listed now, and scripted mode is the default.
- The booth example (a steel ball keeping about 5/7 of mgh as translational KE) ties to the existing ball video, and all of it can be derived on a whiteboard.

Weaknesses:
- Too many hypotheses (H1-H8 plus EC1-EC6), and H1's single-reading clause is nearly true by construction.
- Only 4 held-out clusters.
- S2 samples from the untuned base, so yield may be low, and H4's GRPO clause depends on a P1 run.
- No classical-ML or shuffled-label baseline to answer 'is an LLM needed?'.
- The workstation tier (27B plus the UI) is estimated at 20-23.5 GB, too close to the 24 GB cap.
- E5 has only about 24 runs.
- A physics judge will ask why a ball on two rails keeps less than 5/7, and the student should be ready for that.

grafts: From model-depth: add non-LLM baselines on the held-out experiments: gradient-boosted trees trained on the same computed signature features with signature-type labels, plus a ~20-line rule matcher. This answers the judge's first question, 'is a language model needed at all?'. CPU only, minutes.

From model-depth: a shuffled-label LoRA negative control. Same prompts, cause labels permuted within each experiment, trained with the S1 recipe overnight on the 4B (estimated 1-2 GPU-h). Pre-register that it must gain < 2 pp on held-out experiments, which shows any gain comes from the physics-verified labels and not from exposure to the output format.

From model-depth: draw the S2 rejection samples from the S1 adapter instead of the untuned base, or pre-register both. Time-box every GPU job and set the episode count from throughput measured in its first 10 minutes.

From model-depth: positive controls for the deployment and evaluation pipeline. (1) An adapter-effect check in the 200-case Mac/server parity test: the converted MLX adapter must change outputs wherever the server adapter does. (2) An oracle-in-prompt arm that must score about 100%. (3) A planted duplicate that the leakage checker must catch.

From model-depth: raise the held-out clusters from 4 to 6 by adding two cheap numpy experiments from its held-out list (Atwood machine, lever balance). Report near- vs far-transfer per experiment, with a family-level cluster bootstrap.

From model-depth: 'what must NOT change' equivalence tests for the text-only LoRA, using TOST with pre-registered margins: photo recognition on the open-set image set, and a fixed 300-item general physics set (PhyX, MIT licence).

From wow-product: a deliberately misspecified hi-fi test world as a frozen robustness split, with the in-distribution-to-hi-fi accuracy drop as a pre-registered criterion. Effects the engine never models: pulley inertia and friction, rolling resistance, air drag, string mass, ex-Gaussian timing noise, transcription slips. This is a stronger sim-to-real proxy than noise-only misspecification.

From wow-product: in every real E5 run, measure BOTH the EIG-recommended follow-up and a plain repeat of the last measurement, in script-randomised order. H3 then gets a paired, within-run real-world test (Wilcoxon on the realised entropy reduction).

From wow-product: evidence of independence. The student hand-codes one fault model (e.g., Hooke ruler-zero offset) and checks it against the engine, and the second assistant independently re-implements one two-cause EIG case for cross-checking. Both are logged in the AI ledger.

From wow-product: fix-and-verify. Each verdict gives a quantitative fix with a predicted re-run result (e.g., the intercept should become 0 +/- 0.03 N after rebalancing), and E5 can test that prediction on a subset of runs.

From wow-product: a booth Judge Challenge with paper sabotage cards (no QR codes or URLs), run offline on the 4B tier. Ghost-curve overlays show each suspect's predicted outcome before each extra measurement; precomputed scenarios are the fallback.

From open-set-vision, for the P1 recognition track only, as evaluation and never training: matched-artifact controls on every minimal pair, conformal sets plus one EIG question for the cart+track tie, and a curve of coverage against recalibration with m target photos on the external CC-licensed set. Results are reported per source group as small-n.
must_cut: Hypothesis sprawl in the winner. Keep three confirmatory claims: (1) the atlas, with H1 reframed around which cause pairs the standard multi-point worksheet leaves confounded, since the single-reading clause is nearly true by construction; (2) EIG beats repeat, in simulation and in real runs; (3) the primary H4, S2 vs the untuned base on held-out experiments, reported as a fraction of the oracle. Demote H2, H5-H8 and the S3-vs-S1 GRPO clause to Holm-corrected secondary analyses; EC1-EC6 stay as pass/fail engineering checks.

The 27B workstation tier as a product or booth configuration: 27B plus Streamlit, YOLO and a browser is estimated at 20-23.5 GB, too close to the 24 GB cap. Run the 27B only by itself, in batch, for baselines and parity; the product and demo use the 4B laptop tier.
The 27B NVFP4 arm on the 5090 (vLLM NVFP4 support on consumer Blackwell is unknown). Use the Mac MLX batch subset or GGUF Q4_K_M via llama.cpp instead.

From the 11-14 critical path: the 9B scale point, the Phase-2 vision counterfactual LoRA and the sympy generic-signature compiler. Keep them listed in the research plan as later phases, because nothing can be added after the affiliated fair.
Do not import model-depth's 24-family LabFault scope, its 3-fold family cross-validation, its duplicate 4B tier, its GRPO pilot or its 27B QLoRA.

Do not import open-set-vision's CET training or any in-domain conformal-guarantee claim built on the 809 images (only 3 source videos). Never train on, or display, frames from the downloaded web videos until their provenance and licence are cleared.

Do not import wow-product's 9B GRPO, its 'Too-Perfect Twin' suspect (an implied fabrication accusation is inappropriate in a classroom tool), its classroom sabotage mode or its fault-universe animation before 11-14.

Any model download or continuous job longer than about 1 h before 11-06. Any formal data-generation, training or evaluation run launched by an AI assistant: the student launches each one and logs it in the dated notebook.

Any classroom, teacher-rating or classmate data used as evidence before a 3-member IRB signs Form 4 (the E9 study stays a listed, conditional Phase-3 item). Lessons from 11-07 on are ordinary teaching in scripted mode, with nothing collected.
The fixed 'relative error < 15% = verified' rule, everywhere in product and paper. Replace it with the uncertainty-normalised z agreement.

scores.justification: MEMORY: closes easily. The product runs the 9B MLX 4-bit (5.98 GB, about 8-10 GB in total, estimate) and the 27B is never loaded alongside it. It respects the upload, no-new-photo and LM Studio rules: adapters are served by mlx_vlm.server --adapter-path, with a merge-to-GGUF fallback. SCHEDULE: closes only if nothing fails. In six AI-only days it has to deliver: a 24-family simulator (18 training + 6 held-out families, 3-4 errors each with menus, fixes and bilingual 3-paraphrase templates; the '1.5-2k lines' figure is optimistic), the referee, the evaluation harness, the converter and a full product rework.
